findings.recommendation: Make `context.memory` optional. Replace the enum with generic admission states (off; read-only curated; agent-writable with review) defined in prose in ai-ml-systems §7. Remove `ceiling` from the published schema or define it generically. Replace 'cell' with 'run' everywhere and take ledger row ids out of normative text.

findings.title: Canonical verifier kinds fit one CLI; the library's own packs are 73% custom
findings.quote: | `custom` | Escape hatch — should be rare; high-friction by design. |
findings.critique: The canonical kinds (lockfile_generated, host_registrations_generated, env_canary_not_in_subprocess) describe one command-line wrapper. The library's own five packs use `custom` for 16 of 22 verifiers and a canonical artefact kind once. The 'every skill MUST ship a pack' mandate rests on a claim §1 calls 'a risk hypothesis to test', while the rationale table states it as measured fact.
findings.recommendation: Remove the closed kind enum from the normative surface and keep the kinds as examples. Replace the skill-pack pairing MUST with: every unattended run declares required outputs and at least one deterministic, independently runnable post-run check with a demonstrated failing case. Align the rationale row with §1's hedged wording.

findings.title: Reference verifier passes on a magic word; all skills unevaluated
findings.quote: command: grep -qiE '(unverified|untested|residual risk|not verified|nothing (remains|is) unverified)' ${REPORT}
findings.critique: The reference verifier passes when the report contains a keyword; 'nothing is unverified' passes. Verifier-packs §4 says a stub MUST NOT pass, and this is a stub with a regular expression. All five skills ship `evaluation.evidence: null`, so the hashing and digest checks guarantee byte-identity of prompts nobody has measured. It teaches the wrong lesson about what verification is.
findings.recommendation: Delete keyword-presence assertions or relabel them as lint. Keep only checks that observe artefacts: outputs exist, commands re-run, cited paths resolve. Mark all five skills experimental in the register until one published evaluation exists.

findings.title: Capability tiers A to D are kinds, not a ladder
findings.quote: Teams declare the highest tier they operate in per system and upgrade controls when capability crosses a boundary.
findings.critique: A to D are capability kinds, not a ladder. Fine-tuning (C) is not between retrieval (B) and agents (D); a tool-calling agent with no corpus and no training is 'D' but owes nothing from B or C, while 'Tier B+' and 'Tier A or above' elsewhere assume cumulative order. The library also has skill tiers 0 to 3 and adversarial-testing Tier 0 to 1, so 'tier' alone is ambiguous.
findings.recommendation: Replace the ordinal letters with independent capability flags: calls a model; retrieves from a corpus; trains or fine-tunes; takes actions through tools (split read-only, write, code execution). Key each control to the flag that triggers it. Keep A to D as a legacy alias table for one release.

findings.title: 'Max of capability and materiality' cannot be computed
findings.quote: scale with the max of the two, while the tier table above remains capability-keyed
findings.critique: Materiality has no defined levels: the slice uses 'minimal', 'low', 'high', 'material' and 'critical' with no criteria, so the maximum of a letter and an adjective cannot be computed. A maximum can only raise controls, yet the stated purpose is to stop over-controlling capable, low-stakes systems; the text's own example, a Tier-D agent refactoring fixtures, still lands at D. Two reviewers will classify one system differently.
findings.recommendation: Define three materiality levels with observable criteria, reusing low, material and critical from the applicability overlay (person-affecting, money movement, irreversibility, tenant blast radius). Replace 'max of the two' with a control matrix: one row per control, with the capability flag and minimum materiality that trigger it.

findings.title: Dedicated-principal trigger swallows its own exception; 'per-agent' undefined
findings.quote: (Tier D, write access to production, or unattended operation at material blast radius) MUST act under a **dedicated per-agent principal**
findings.critique: Tier D is defined as any agent with tools and side effects, which is every agent this subsection covers, so the 'lower-autonomy agents MAY share a team principal' branch is empty as written. 'Per-agent' is also undefined: per definition, per deployment, or per running instance? Identity providers distinguish a definition-level blueprint from the instance identities created under it; the rule does not say which level satisfies it, and the answer changes cost and revocation behaviour for a fleet.
findings.recommendation: Trigger the dedicated-principal MUST on write authority to production or regulated data, money movement, or unattended operation, not on 'Tier D'. Define 'per-agent' as per agent definition and environment, with run or instance identity carried as a harness-stamped session attribute.

findings.title: Dual-LLM architecture mandated for every tool-using agent
findings.quote: Architectural defence is not optional for Tier D systems.
findings.critique: The mandated design keeps raw external content away from the planner, but §1.2's own loop has the planner observe tool output, and a coding or browsing agent cannot work otherwise. The cited implementation is a research artefact; no general-purpose harness ships it. Controls teams can deploy today (remove one leg of the trifecta, sandbox with egress allowlist, approval on exfiltration-capable actions) are relegated to an interim 'practical minimum'.
findings.recommendation: Retype: where all three trifecta legs are present, the system MUST apply at least one deterministic control that breaks the exfiltration or action path: remove a leg, egress allowlist, capability or taint policy in code, or human approval bound to the exact action. Present dual-LLM as one conforming design among several and make §9.3 the baseline.

findings.title: Typed tool output presented as an injection control
findings.quote: - Structure tool outputs as typed structured data (not raw text) so the model reads values, not instructions.
findings.critique: Wrapping attacker-controlled text in a structured field does not stop the model reading it as instructions; a string is a string. Typing helps only when the value is constrained (enumeration, number, validated identifier) or is never shown to the planning model. As written the bullet tells teams that schema-shaped tool results are an injection control, which they are not.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: 'Constrain what untrusted sources can return to the planner: enumerations, numbers, validated identifiers, length-capped fields. Free-text fields from untrusted sources remain untrusted input however they are wrapped and need one of the deterministic controls in this section.'

findings.title: No owner mandates sandboxed execution and egress control for agents
findings.quote: doctrine does not currently mandate sandboxed execution
findings.critique: The most effective control for agents that run shell commands or generated code is absent from every canonical owner and admitted as a gap here. It exists only as a checklist item ('isolated preview/test environment without standing production credentials') and a tooling row, which by the layering rules cannot create an obligation. The production-database deletion cited in §6.1 is this failure.
findings.recommendation: Add to ai-ml-systems §4, typed: agents that execute code or shell commands in estate-governed paths MUST run in an isolated environment with filesystem scope limited to the workspace, default-deny network egress with an allowlist, and no production-write or long-lived credentials; SHOULD for local single-user work. Evidence: reviewed sandbox configuration plus a negative test.

findings.title: Interactive agents inherit every developer credential
findings.quote: A tool acting entirely under a human's interactive session is that human's session, governed by §3
findings.critique: The dominant deployment, a coding agent in a developer's terminal, is carved out of agent identity and inherits every credential the developer holds: cloud sessions, production database URLs, SSH agent, package-publish tokens. §3 covers only multi-factor and just-in-time elevation for people. The best-documented agent incidents happened in exactly this mode, as agentic-loop §6.1 itself notes.
findings.recommendation: Add one bullet: an agent operating in a person's interactive session SHOULD run with a credential set narrower than the person's (scoped tokens, environment allowlist, no production-write credentials) and MUST NOT be handed production-mutating credentials without the approval gate of ai-ml-systems §4. Cross-link the sandbox rule.

findings.title: Carve-out excludes the attack the section cites
findings.quote: An instruction file consumed only by an interactive assistant operating under
findings.critique: The carve-out classes interactive assistants' rules files as ordinary repository content, but the rules-file backdoor cited in §2 targeted exactly those files in interactive editors. Repository-carried agent configuration (rules files, tool-server configuration, hooks) acts with the developer's authority as soon as the repository is opened. The evidence the section cites sits outside the scope the section protects.
findings.recommendation: Keep the full pipeline-definition treatment for privileged automation, and add a floor for every repository: agent configuration paths have code owners, CI rejects hidden or bidirectional Unicode in them, and changes to tool-server or hook configuration get explicit review. Add: agent configuration in an untrusted clone is untrusted input.

findings.title: Tool poisoning and post-approval tool changes left informative
findings.quote: - **Consult published hardening baselines** *(informative)*:
findings.critique: The normative tool-protocol rules cover revision pinning, OAuth and an allowlist. The attack class that has actually hit users, poisoned tool descriptions, definitions that change after approval, and one server shadowing another's tools, is left to an informative 'consult'. Tool descriptions and results are third-party model input; an allowlisted server can still change them tomorrow.
findings.recommendation: Add a typed bullet: hosts in estate-governed paths SHOULD pin approved tool definitions (name, description, schema) by hash and require re-approval on change; tool descriptions and results are untrusted input under the §7 rule; third-party server packages are version- or digest-pinned. Leave the baselines informative for the rest.

findings.title: Client-side resource indicator stated; server-side audience validation omitted
findings.quote: clients MUST send RFC 8707 resource indicators so tokens are audience-bound to one server
findings.critique: Sending a resource indicator binds nothing if the authorisation server ignores it. The pinned revision puts the binding control on the server: it MUST validate that the token was issued for it as audience and MUST NOT accept or transit other tokens. The library states the client half and the passthrough ban but omits the server-side validation duty that makes them effective.
findings.recommendation: Add: 'servers MUST validate that each access token was issued for that server as audience and reject tokens issued for any other resource', citing the pinned revision's token-handling section.

findings.title: OAuth-only rule outlaws mutual-TLS internal tool servers
findings.quote: A remote or multi-tenant MCP server MUST implement the OAuth 2.1 resource-server model against an external identity provider (no bespoke token schemes
findings.critique: Stricter than the pinned revision, which makes authorisation OPTIONAL and says HTTP implementations SHOULD conform. It also outlaws an internal tool server authenticated by mutual TLS or platform workload identity, the mechanism zero-trust §1 itself prefers for service-to-service calls. A team with a mesh-authenticated internal server would need an exception to do the right thing.
findings.recommendation: Retype: a remote server MUST authenticate every caller with a standard mechanism and authorise per tool. Where clients act for users or come from outside the estate, that mechanism MUST be the pinned revision's OAuth resource-server model. Service-to-service callers inside the estate MAY use mutual TLS or workload identity per zero-trust §§1-2.

findings.title: Slopsquat gate is enforced after the package has installed
findings.quote: the existing CI dependency-review gate and lockfile-diff review are the forcing function that surfaces and blocks the diff, not the test
findings.critique: By the time a pull request exists, an agent has already run the install on a workstation or runner and install scripts have executed; the forcing function fires after the harm. 'First introduced by a model' is not observable at the diff. 'Download history' is gameable, and §8 of the supply-chain file bans it as evidence for models. The intent is right; the enforcement point is a manual lookup nobody can audit.
findings.recommendation: Trigger on any new dependency name, whoever proposed it. Make enforcement technical: a registry proxy or allowlist, a package-manager minimum-release-age setting, install scripts off by default, and a harness hook intercepting install commands in agent sessions. Keep the manual lookup as the solo-developer fallback. Drop download counts as evidence.

findings.title: No rule to pin model versions or alert on a changed responding model
findings.quote: A silent model upgrade is a **change to your system** (§3 regression triggers).
findings.critique: The library treats silent model change as a contract and telemetry matter but never states the engineering rule: production calls name an immutable model version, not a floating alias. The run-contract examples use `provider/model-default`. Observability §7.1 records the responding model, but nothing requires an alert when it differs or an evaluation run before a new version is promoted.
findings.recommendation: Add to ai-ml-systems §6, typed: production and estate-governed calls MUST reference the provider's immutable model version where one is offered; a floating alias is a recorded exception. Promotion to a new version is a change with a golden-set regression run. Alert when responding and requested models differ. Track provider retirement dates in the inventory.

findings.title: Per-call 'explicit reasoning' mandate is a 2022 prompting technique
findings.quote: - Every **tool call must be preceded by explicit reasoning** about why.
findings.critique: This encodes a 2022 prompting technique as a universal rule. Current models reason internally, often with hidden or summarised reasoning, and issue parallel tool calls; a harness cannot observe or enforce explicit reasoning per call. The principle file says private chain-of-thought is neither required nor accepted as evidence, so the rule conflicts with its parent. Nobody could tell whether a system complies.
findings.recommendation: Delete the two 'must' bullets and the 'not optional commentary' sentence. Keep the enforceable part of §1.2: an iteration cap and budget stop enforced by the harness, and logged tool calls with inputs and results.

findings.title: Undefined private acronym 'ISC' is an autonomy trigger in a principle
findings.quote: earn greater autonomy from empirical ISC pass-rate data
findings.critique: 'ISC' (Ideal State Criteria) is one author's personal-assistant framework term. It appears undefined in the principle's Tier D row, is absent from the glossary and from ADR 0046's vocabulary list, and is the trigger for moving the autonomy slider. The standard terms are acceptance criteria and evaluation pass rate. The pattern adds an unsourced 'answerable in under 2 seconds' test and bars criteria needing human judgement.
findings.recommendation: Replace 'ISC' with 'acceptance criteria' throughout and 'ISC pass rate' with 'verified task success rate'. Delete the two-second rule. Allow human-judged criteria when a named reviewer and rubric are declared. Credit the source once in References.

findings.title: Agentic-loop-design stacks five documents; about a quarter is rules
findings.quote: | **Minimal** | Acknowledgment, clarification request, a rating, a greeting | Direct response; no tooling |
findings.critique: §10 documents one chat assistant's request router (greetings, ratings, an undefined LEARN phase); it is not loop doctrine. The file runs to 7,100 words because it stacks five documents: a 2023-era loop tutorial (§§1-4), context engineering, judge validation, graph decomposition and an OWASP crosswalk. The rules a team needs (§6.1 item 3, §8.3, §9.3-9.4 and the §8.2 MUSTs) are about a quarter of it.
findings.recommendation: Cut §4, §10 and the §12 rows that duplicate ai-ml-systems §8. Reduce §§1-3 to one section on iteration caps, external verification and declared acceptance criteria. Move §8.2 to a judge-validation pattern, §8.4 to a decomposition pattern and §11 to a reference page. Target about 200 lines.

findings.title: Autonomy-slider MUST is ambiguous and mixes two axes
findings.quote: action MUST start at "approve before irreversible" regardless of agent maturity
findings.critique: 'Start at ... regardless of maturity' does not say whether the position may ever move. The slider puts two things on one axis: approving live actions and reviewing proposed diffs. A coding agent whose auth change goes through pull-request review sits at 'review results before apply', right of the mandated position, so it breaches this MUST while satisfying the principle. The last rung, 'deployed silently', contradicts the principle's ban on silent production mutation.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: for these action classes a named human MUST approve before the effect reaches a shared or production system, at every maturity level; this never relaxes. Separate the two axes (runtime action approval; change-path review). Rename the last rung 'unattended with post-hoc review' and list the action classes that can never reach it.

findings.title: A MUST rests on a preprint arXiv has withdrawn
findings.quote: runs 33–41 percentage points and reorders judge rankings ([arXiv 2606.19544](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19544))
findings.critique: arXiv administrators withdrew this paper on 2026-11-03 for not meeting research content quality standards. It is the headline evidence for a MUST, is cited again in the anti-pattern table and references, and its 33-41 point figure applied to one benchmark only. A library that grades sources cannot leave a withdrawn preprint under a normative rule. The rule also mandates kappa when a gate's decision-relevant measure is its false-pass rate.
findings.recommendation: Remove the citation and figure in all three places and rest the rule on the remaining sources. Reword the duty: report the confusion matrix with per-class error rates (false pass, false fail) plus a chance-corrected statistic of the estate's choice. Add a reference-status check (withdrawn, retracted, superseded) to the periodic sweep.

findings.title: Unsourced, inconsistent context-fill thresholds and a 'dominant failure mode' claim
findings.quote: Model quality degrades steeply at 90%+ context fill.
findings.critique: The principle says 90%, the pattern's anti-pattern table says 95%; neither cites a source, and degradation with context length is gradual and model-specific. The same file asserts that context failures are 'now the dominant agent failure mode', supported in the pattern by a social-media post held under an evidence exception. Numbers and superlatives like these date within one model generation.
findings.recommendation: Replace both thresholds with: 'quality degrades as context fills; set a compaction threshold from your own evaluation'. Reword the dominance claim to 'a common failure class' or cite a study.

findings.title: Volatile facts sit in pattern bodies with no as-of or review-by marker
findings.quote: outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal eval
findings.critique: Pattern bodies embed facts with short half-lives: a vendor's internal benchmark on mid-2025 models, 2022-23 results used to assert that loop structure beats model choice, named incident products' default modes, and regulatory dates. The 'Standards watch' paragraphs show the right habit (dated, labelled informative), but 'Why' paragraphs carry the same kind of fact and read as timeless.
findings.recommendation: Adopt one convention: any sentence carrying a benchmark figure, product behaviour, draft-standard status or calendar date sits in a block with an as-of date and a review-by date, or moves to a dated evidence note linked from the rule. Sweeps fail on expired review-by dates. Delete the 'Every time' quotation in §4.

findings.title: Limits, stops and delegation enforced outside the model
findings.quote: - **Bound the tree** — fan-out, depth, time, token/compute/cost, and retry limits MUST be enforced outside model prompts.
findings.critique: §8.3 and §6.1 item 3 are the rules that would have stopped the documented runaway-loop and ignored-instruction incidents: limits and stops live in the harness, authority only narrows on delegation, resume revalidates, cancellation revokes. They are harness-agnostic, typed and checkable with a negative test. A length cut must not dilute them.
findings.recommendation: Keep verbatim. When the file is shortened, move these rules to the top.

findings.title: Pattern adoption is not evidence; adaptive evaluation required
findings.quote: Deploying the §9 architecture is a **design control**, not evidence of effectiveness.
findings.critique: The rule refuses to let adoption of a design stand in for evidence and demands attacker-iterates evaluation with repeat trials against the actual deployment. The headline source was confirmed on the publisher's page. This is ahead of most internal security standards and gives a reviewer a concrete question to ask of any claimed injection defence.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written, including the minimum viable form in testing-strategy §5.

findings.title: Schema-neutral per-call telemetry minimum with content capture off
findings.quote: the requested model **and** the provider-reported responding model where they can differ; the responding model is the pricing and behaviour key.
findings.critique: A per-call minimum (requested and responding model, split token counts, run correlation, tool-call ids) that names no attribute schema, defaults content capture off, and states its own control record. It is the detection half of silent model change and runaway spend, cheap on any telemetry stack, and testable on sampled traces.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written. Add only the alert on requested-versus-responding mismatch proposed in SAI-19.

findings.title: Model artefacts admitted like code, with safe formats required
findings.quote: Production model loading MUST use **non-executable weight formats** (**safetensors**-class: tensor data only, no deserialization hooks).
findings.critique: §8 turns model artefacts into ordinary dependencies with crisp, testable rules: digest pinning, safe formats, a sandboxed exception path, scanners treated as evadable, popularity barred as evidence. It closes a well-documented code-execution path and names its exception route instead of softening the rule.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written. Apply the same 'popularity is not evidence' reasoning to package admission in §7.

findings.title: Named sponsor, orphan disablement and an honest standards watch
findings.quote: an **orphaned** agent — one with no current sponsor — is disabled, not left running
findings.critique: A named sponsor with a lifecycle and orphan disablement is implementable today: one major identity provider ships agent identities with sponsor-transfer workflows (confirmed on its documentation), and elsewhere tags plus an offboarding job suffice. The dated, informative 'standards watch' is the right way to carry pre-final material. The agent financial default-deny in cost-and-finops §7.1 is equally sound.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written; fix only the trigger wording raised in SAI-09.

findings.title: Lifecycle pattern unchanged at 4,084 words; ADR 0047 never executed
findings.quote: S0-S10 remains a useful diagnostic decomposition for evidence invalidation and audit reconstruction.
findings.critique: Still 4,084 words and eighteen sections; ADR 0047, targeting 1,600 words and nine, is Proposed and unexecuted. One file carries seven gates, eleven states, eight evidence classes, six adoption stages, five record families, seven claim types, six mandate classes and three closure modes. Rules live in §3, §5, §9 and one bullet of §13; §§2, 6-8, 10-12 and 14-18 restate them or are taxonomy, diagram and migration history.
findings.recommendation: Execute ADR 0047 or withdraw it. Keep scope, invariants, the gate table with minimum evidence, transition admissibility, the closed-authority-loop rule and failure modes. Move S0-S10, E0-E7, record families, claim model, diagram, brownfield stages, measures and §18 to a companion note.

findings.title: Seven gates apply to every AI-assisted change with no stated floor
findings.quote: A low-materiality change may cross several in one pull request, but it does not skip their obligations.
findings.critique: Scope is any change where AI 'drafts or changes executable intent', which in 2026 is most pull requests. Each must then show G2's typed candidate and runtime claims, invariants, threat and abuse cases, evidence obligations, validity windows and owners. The pattern never states what satisfies the gates for a routine change, so a reviewer cannot tell compliance from non-compliance and a small team cannot tell where to stop.
findings.recommendation: Add a floor after the gate table: for a low-materiality change, a pull-request description stating why and what, passing required checks and one accountable review discharge G1-G7; typed claims, threat cases and observation windows apply from 'material' upward. Give one worked example per level.

findings.title: ADR 0046 vocabulary still present, including a term it says was retired
findings.quote: | `authority` | yes | `filesystem`, `env`, `network`, `subprocess` — typed-denial defaults. |
findings.critique: ADR 0046, still Proposed, says 'typed denial' was retired as executed editorial work, yet the hyphenated form survives twice here. 'Enactment', 'mandate class', 'closure mode' and 'record families' remain throughout the lifecycle pattern and glossary, and 'estate' compounds have grown rather than shrunk. A reader must still learn a dialect before reaching a rule.
findings.recommendation: Finish the retired-now batch: replace both uses with 'explicit deny by default'. Decide ADR 0046: accept and execute it with ADR 0047, or reject it and record why. Add 'ISC' and 'cell' to its term list.

findings.title: Bank three-lines model offered as a default for any team, with no scale-down
findings.quote: Reconcile the inventory **on material change and at least quarterly**
findings.critique: The pattern transplants a bank's three-lines model (first-line owner, second-line challenge, exit game days, tracked literacy) and calls it portable defaults for any team. It never says what a five-person team or a solo developer does. The test matrix applies continuous input-distribution drift monitoring to 'all production models', justified by an EU AI Act article that binds only high-risk systems. The quarterly cadence has no source.
findings.recommendation: Add an applicability section: below 'material', the floor is an inventory entry (owner, data classes, provider), an acceptable-use note and the change-path rules. Independent challenge, fairness testing, exit plans and game days start at 'material' or person-affecting. For hosted-model systems restate drift as pinned version plus sampled online evaluation.

findings.title: 'In force' is the wrong term and the transitional date expires in two weeks
findings.quote: In force **2026-08-02**; Art 50(2) providers already on the market before that date have a transitional deadline of **2026-12-02**.
findings.critique: The dates agree with current commentary on the amending regulation, but 'in force' is the wrong term: the Act entered into force in 2024 and Article 50 applies from 2026-08-02. The transitional sentence becomes history two weeks after this review. Regulatory calendar facts repeated in a principle and a pattern will drift apart.
findings.recommendation: Say 'applies from'. Keep dates only in privacy-and-data-governance §5.4 with an as-of marker and link to it from here. After 2026-12-02 delete the transitional clause.
findings.external_basis: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/ (application date); the 2026-12-02 transitional date was seen only in secondary search results, not checked on the Official Journal

findings.title: Retrieval isolation is one sentence and stops at the tenant
findings.quote: same rigor as row-level security for a multi-tenant DB
findings.critique: One sentence covers the hardest part of enterprise retrieval. It addresses tenants but not users: the common leak is a user retrieving documents inside their own tenant that they may not read. Nothing says the filter must be enforced in the retrieval layer with the caller's identity, before ranking; the principle hedges with 'where possible'. Permission changes and deletions at source have no propagation requirement and no isolation test is named.
findings.recommendation: Add typed rules: retrieval MUST apply the requesting identity's tenant and document-level entitlements as a hard filter inside the retrieval layer, never by prompt or after ranking; permission revocation and source deletion propagate to every index within a declared interval; a cross-tenant and cross-user negative test runs on index or filter change.

findings.title: No control for exfiltration through rendered output or for corpus write trust
findings.quote: Mitigations: **instruction** hardening, **output** policy, **tool** least privilege
findings.critique: The list leads with instruction hardening, the weakest control, and leaves 'output policy' undefined. The channel most often exploited in retrieval systems without tools is the rendered answer: injected content makes the model emit a link or image whose address carries private data. The baseline also never says that write access to the corpus is write access to the prompt, so ingestion sources need a trust decision.
findings.recommendation: Add: where context holds non-public data, rendered model output MUST NOT auto-load remote resources or carry links to hosts outside an allowlist. Record a source and trust level for every ingested document and exclude or down-rank untrusted sources for sensitive uses. Move instruction hardening last and label it defence in depth.

findings.title: Evaluation is untyped and ungated; freshness has no section
findings.quote: run **regression** on **retrieval** when changing chunking, embeddings, fusion, or corpus
findings.critique: The heading says non-negotiable but nothing is typed and no evidence is named. The golden set has no unanswerable queries, so a system that always answers looks perfect. Model and prompt changes are not triggers, no threshold gates release, and the set is never refreshed from real traffic. Freshness, which the principle calls an explicit SLA, has no section and no observable measure here.
findings.recommendation: Type it: production retrieval MUST have a versioned golden set including no-answer cases, run on corpus, chunking, embedding, reranker, prompt or model change, with declared thresholds gating promotion. Add a freshness section: index lag as a metric with an alert, and source-deletion propagation time.

findings.title: Ban on tool co-author trailers is a preference typed as MUST
findings.quote: A non-human tool **MUST NOT** be named in an authorship field (`Author`, `Co-Authored-By`, or any successor conferring authorship standing)
findings.critique: A stance on credit is promoted to a universal MUST with no failure evidence. Common assistants add a co-author trailer by default, hosted coding agents commit under bot identities the user cannot change, and many organisations use those markers to measure and audit AI-assisted change. The replacement 'curated' class claims to be falsifiable against the diff, but no pre-revision artefact is kept, so nobody can check it.
findings.recommendation: Retype to the durable rule: every merged change MUST have a named accountable human, and AI involvement MUST be recoverable in estate-governed paths. Make the mechanism an estate choice (trailer, method record, or platform metadata). Reduce the class vocabulary to assisted or not, plus tool identity; keep three classes as MAY.

findings.title: Maintainer doctrine about serving this library sits in the consumer path
findings.quote: - No conforming server is named or shipped here, by design; conformance is
findings.critique: This pattern governs how a tool server exposes this library to agents. No such server is shipped or verified, tier 2-3 skills are 'roadmap rows, not files', and the page says it changes nothing for consumers. It is maintainer doctrine in the consumer path, routed from the umbrella and injected as an unnumbered bullet into the AI principle. ADR 0047's maintainers split would move it; that ADR is unexecuted.
findings.recommendation: Move the pattern, the skills register and the contract schemas it references under a maintainers area. Remove the umbrella route and the orphan bullet between §7 and §8 of ai-ml-systems. Keep one generic sentence in §7: tool servers return cited, revision-pinned excerpts and expose no direct write path.

findings.title: 'Agent-ready' profile mandates human autocomplete, omits agent operability
findings.quote: Every manifest row **MUST** provide autocomplete appropriate to its primary
findings.critique: Shell completion and command palettes are human affordances; agents discover a tool through help output and schemas. The profile mandates them, with no per-release waiver, while omitting what makes software operable by an agent: non-interactive mode, machine-readable output, stable exit codes, dry-run, idempotent retries and structured errors. It reads as one product family's release checklist.
findings.recommendation: Rename it for what it is (skill and completion shipping profile), or replace the autocomplete MUST with agent-operability properties: non-interactive operation, structured output and errors, documented exit codes, dry-run for mutating commands, machine-readable command schema. Make completion a SHOULD for command-line tools only.

findings.title: 150 lines of machinery around a six-line prompt
findings.quote: Priming needs a sibling verifier that checks presence and integrity of the
findings.critique: One hundred and fifty lines, a schema kind, a hash scheme and an evaluation contract surround a six-line prompt that the pattern itself says proves nothing. The verifier needs the rendered system prompt, which hosted assistants do not expose. The useful content is §1: self-review is not independent evidence. §8 is a migration note about a rule that new consumers never saw.
findings.recommendation: Fold §1 into agentic-loop-design's verification rule and §3's evaluation caution into run-contracts §3.5. Keep the prompt as a non-normative example. Delete §§4, 5 and 8 and take the `priming_active` kind off the normative surface.

findings.title: Privileged-automation reference ends without telling the engineer what to do
findings.quote: | Declare scope | For a governed run, write the contract: closed tool set, deny-by-default authority, required outputs, and verifier packs. |
findings.critique: The umbrella sends anyone asking about agents here first, and the page ends without telling them what to type. 'Write the contract' has no example, no harness mapping and no minimum; ten invariants restate the owners. The opening also confirms that an interactive assistant running tools is a governed run, importing the proportionality problem. The git-worktrees reference, by contrast, is concrete and usable.
findings.recommendation: Add three worked minimums: a supervised developer session, a CI agent job and a scheduled agent, each showing identity, tool and path scope, network policy, limits, approval points and evidence in generic settings. Cut the invariants to the five a reader must not get wrong and link the rest.

findings.title: Memory writes MUST be 'validated' with no definition of validation
findings.quote: Writes to persistent memory MUST be validated and provenance-tagged (writing identity, run, timestamp) before they become retrievable
findings.critique: 'Validated' is never defined. The text defers to a schema enumeration whose only substantive mode is operator-signed memory, a design ordinary memory features lack, and the library says elsewhere that a model-based filter is not a defence. An assessor cannot say whether a product's memory feature complies, so teams will either switch memory off or claim compliance with a provenance tag alone.
findings.recommendation: Name the acceptable validations: human or operator approval before promotion; deterministic checks (schema, source allowlist, size limits, rejection of content from untrusted sources); or quarantine with delayed promotion and sampled review. State that a model-based filter alone does not satisfy the MUST. Define the modes in prose here, not in the contract schema.

findings.title: Patch releases may carry additive behaviour, contradicting SemVer
findings.quote: - Additive behaviour that does not break existing workflows or contracts
findings.critique: SemVer 2.0.0 limits a patch to backward-compatible bug fixes and requires a minor for any new backward-compatible functionality. This bullet, and the short-reference row 'safe additions', allow additions in patches. Consumers who pin to a patch range then receive new surface they did not accept, and cannot safely move down within the range. A policy that says it follows SemVer must not redefine its smallest unit.
findings.recommendation: Delete the bullet. Change the Short Reference patch row to 'backward-compatible bug fixes only'. In section 3 say additions and deprecation markers require a minor (SemVer items 6 and 7). If a deviation is intended, label it as a deviation from the specification.

findings.title: Missing (rank 6 of 7): published versions are immutable; public API is declared
findings.quote: ## 8. Release Hygiene
findings.critique: The policy omits two SemVer requirements it depends on: a released version's contents must not be modified, and software using SemVer must declare its public API. Without the first, tags can be moved and packages republished under an existing version, which also defeats pinning as a supply-chain control. Without the second, 'classify by consumer impact' has nothing to be measured against.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 8: a published version, tag or digest MUST NOT be modified or re-pointed; correct a bad release by publishing a new version and withdrawing the old one. Add to section 1: each unit SHOULD state where its public API is declared. Where the ecosystem has an API-diff tool, run it in the release gate as evidence for the bump.

findings.title: Hotfix path is release-first with merge-back and no forward-port check
findings.quote: **Hotfixes** branch from the tagged release, fix, tag patch, merge back to `main` so drift does not accumulate.
findings.critique: The fix reaches production from the release line before trunk has it. If the merge back is forgotten or conflicts, the next trunk release reintroduces the bug; nothing here detects that. Trunk-based guidance says the opposite: reproduce and fix on trunk, then cherry-pick to the release line, and do not merge release branches back. Merging a release line into main also imports release-only commits.
findings.recommendation: Make trunk-first the SHOULD default: fix on trunk with a test, cherry-pick to the release line, build and verify a new candidate. Permit release-first only when the bug cannot be reproduced on trunk or recovery cannot wait, with a tracked forward-port that blocks the next release from trunk. Update impl/branching-and-integration.md and the release checklist to match.

findings.title: Release branches exist only as a legal-owned LTS exception
findings.quote: maintain a **named** `release/X.y` or `support/vN` branch with **documented** EOL
findings.critique: The only supported-line model is a years-long branch whose exception is owned by security and legal review. Ordinary release branches are absent: cut a few days before a release for app-store, on-premises or packaged software, or kept for the previous major of a library. Open-source maintainers run these routinely. A team that needs one must either claim an LTS exception or ignore the pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'release branch' case separate from LTS: cut late from trunk, no feature work, fixes arrive by cherry-pick from trunk, a tag marks each release, the branch is deleted when the release leaves support, and the release owner is accountable. Keep security and legal ownership for regulator- or contract-driven LTS only.

findings.title: 'Trunk-based' is defined looser than the research it borrows from
findings.quote: - **Short-lived topic branches** exist only long enough to produce a reviewable change. Days, not weeks.
findings.critique: DORA's trunk-based capability measures three or fewer active branches, merging to trunk at least daily, branches that typically last hours, no code freezes, and synchronous review. This file sets 'days, not weeks' with async-first pull-request review. That is short-lived feature branching: a reasonable default, but not the practice the cited delivery outcomes were measured on. High-performing trunk teams would not recognise it as theirs.
findings.recommendation: State the research threshold as the SHOULD target (integrate to trunk at least daily; three or fewer active branches) and keep 'a few days' as the outer limit that forces a split. Name the observable evidence: branch age at merge and active-branch count. If the looser default is deliberate, call it short-lived branching and say why.

findings.title: Required-review rule cannot be met by a solo maintainer and ignores pairing
findings.quote: at least one approval from someone who was not the sole author of the change, except for documented bot-only or emergency paths.
findings.critique: Untyped and universal, with exceptions only for bots and emergencies. A single maintainer cannot obtain an approval from someone else, and the adoption playbook, which expects solo-maintained use, does not say what replaces it. Paired or ensemble work, which DORA treats as valid synchronous review, earns no credit. A baseline rule its first reader must break teaches readers to discount the rest.
findings.recommendation: Type it: SHOULD for repositories with two or more maintainers; MUST where separation of duties is an external obligation or for the high-risk classes in the review pattern. For single-maintainer repositories name the substitute (enforced required checks plus a recorded self-review against the description). Count recorded pairing as review.

findings.title: Missing (rank 3 of 7): what happens when trunk goes red
findings.quote: - Keep **one integration branch** (`main`) always deployable or clearly marked otherwise.
findings.critique: 'Clearly marked otherwise' is an escape hatch with no marker, owner or time limit, and no file in this slice says what a team does when the protected branch fails after merge. DORA's continuous-integration capability is specific: fixing the build takes priority over other work, and if it cannot be fixed in minutes the breaking change is identified and reverted.
findings.recommendation: Delete 'or clearly marked otherwise'. Add to collaboration.md section 2: when the protected branch fails its gate, restoring it takes priority over new merges; the breaking change SHOULD be reverted if no fix lands within an estate-set short window. Evidence: time from red to green on the protected branch.

findings.title: Missing (rank 5 of 7): no latency expectation for the required gate
findings.quote: - Slow full gates are acceptable when paired with a **fast inner loop** that catches common mistakes before review.
findings.critique: This is the only statement about gate duration, and it sets no bound. DORA's continuous-integration capability says tests should give feedback in a few minutes, with an upper limit of about ten. A required gate that takes most of an hour makes small pull requests, merge queues and daily integration impractical, and a fast inner loop does not shorten the wait to merge.
findings.recommendation: Add a SHOULD with an estate-tunable default: required pre-merge checks finish in about ten minutes at the median; slower suites move to post-merge or scheduled surfaces with a named owner. Add median required-gate duration to the scorecard's optional metrics.

findings.title: Missing (rank 1 of 7): unreviewed changes must not run with secrets or privilege
findings.quote: are **in the same trust class** as application code for review and static analysis
findings.critique: The principle treats pipeline definitions as reviewable code but never says that a run triggered by an unreviewed change, especially from a fork, must not receive secrets or write-scoped tokens. That is poisoned pipeline execution, OWASP CICD-SEC-4, and it is the main hazard of accepting outside contributions. In this library it appears only as a risk name in a GitOps source table and an aside in an illustrative tooling page.
findings.recommendation: Add an invariant: a pipeline run triggered by a change that has not passed review MUST NOT receive secrets, deploy credentials or write-scoped tokens, and MUST NOT execute that change's pipeline definitions with privilege. Runs for first-time external contributors SHOULD need maintainer approval. Evidence: trigger and token-permission configuration.

findings.title: Missing (rank 4 of 7): third-party pipeline steps pinned to immutable references
findings.quote: CI job graphs, release workflows, packaging hooks, and **third-party** steps they invoke
findings.critique: The definition brings third-party steps into scope, yet no invariant says they must be referenced immutably. The only statement is item 4 of a tooling page marked illustrative. A shared CI step referenced by a movable tag lets its publisher, or whoever compromises the publisher, run new code with the pipeline's credentials on the next build, with no change to review.
findings.recommendation: Add to invariant 2: third-party steps, reusable workflows and build containers used on release or deploy paths MUST be referenced by commit, digest or the host's dependency lock, and SHOULD be so referenced elsewhere; updates arrive as reviewed changes. Cross-link dependencies-supply-chain.md section 1.

findings.title: Missing (rank 2 of 7): approval is bound to the revision that was reviewed
findings.quote: You share post-merge ownership of outcomes for the scope you approved, within team norms.
findings.critique: Nothing ties an approval to the reviewed revision. An author can gain approval, push further commits and merge; the approved change and the merged change then differ, and 'the scope you approved' means nothing. Mainstream hosts offer stale-approval dismissal and approval of the most recent push by someone other than the pusher, but both are optional settings and administrators are exempt by default.
findings.recommendation: Add to merge-path invariant 1: an approval applies to the reviewed revision; a material change after approval needs fresh approval from someone other than the person who pushed it (SHOULD at baseline, MUST for the high-risk classes in section 5), and bypass by administrators is disabled or logged. List the host settings in tooling/collaboration.md.

findings.title: Authorship-field prohibition is a MUST the hosting platform breaks by default
findings.quote: A non-human tool **MUST NOT** be named in an authorship field (`Author`, `Co-Authored-By`, or any successor conferring authorship standing)
findings.critique: The adopter often does not control these fields. Hosted coding agents commit under their own bot identity, and squash merging can add a co-author trailer for every commit author. A MUST the platform violates by default cannot be enforced without rewriting history. Section 2 of this file also says the reviewer shares ownership of the outcome, which contradicts 'held whole' by the author.
findings.recommendation: Keep as the MUST what matters: every merged change has a named accountable human. Retype the field rule to SHOULD NOT for fields the author controls, state how platform-set bot identities are handled (accountable human recorded on the change request), and reconcile the wording with the reviewer's shared ownership in section 2.

findings.title: Method-record class is self-declared; 'falsifiable' is not true
findings.quote: it claims the harness and ruleset were pinned and the output materially revised, and it is falsifiable by reading the diff against the cited revisions
findings.critique: A reviewer sees the final diff, not the model output it was revised from, so 'materially revised' cannot be tested by reading the diff. The boundary between 'ordinary tool assistance' and `generated` is undefined for multi-line agent completions. A MUST whose only evidence is the author's own label is an attestation; describing it as falsifiable overstates what the control proves.
findings.recommendation: Either reduce to one observable fact recorded by tooling (an agent harness produced the candidate, with its identity and revision), or keep three classes as a SHOULD and call them the author's attestation. Define the boundary by something observable, such as whether the tool or the person initiated the change set.

findings.title: Regulated change approval is conceded, not designed
findings.quote: Regulated sectors or customer contracts may add approvals **outside** the PR
findings.critique: This sentence is the whole treatment of regulated change. It accepts an approval outside the merge path instead of showing how the merge path meets the obligation. DORA's guidance says peer review can satisfy segregation of duties and that it found no evidence that formal external review lowers change failure. The pattern's central position against advisory boards cites only a code-review style guide.
findings.recommendation: Add a regulated profile: segregation of duties is met by host-enforced author-is-not-approver, approval bound to the revision, pipeline-only enactment and retained evidence; an advisory board keeps coordination and the highest-risk classes. Cite DORA's change-approval capability as the evidence for the pattern's position.

findings.title: Missing (rank 7 of 7): technique for long-running replacements on trunk
findings.quote: ## Feature Work Without Blocking Trunk
findings.critique: Long-running work gets three bullets: slices, flags, contract versioning. Replacing a component or framework over months is the case that most often pushes teams back to long-lived branches, and the standard answers, branch by abstraction for a component and a strangler boundary for a system, are not named here. The adoption playbook mentions the strangler idea once, for legacy monoliths only.
findings.recommendation: Add a fourth item: when a replacement cannot sit behind one flag, introduce an abstraction on trunk, build the new implementation behind it, move callers in small merges, then delete the old implementation and the abstraction if it no longer earns its place. Link data-and-migrations.md expand and contract for the stateful part.

findings.title: Promotion gate blocks on any new disclosure, at any severity
findings.quote: A previously green merge path does **not** authorise promotion after **new** disclosures unless an explicit, **scoped** exception or **VEX**-style exploitability record is attached to the evidence bundle
findings.critique: Untyped and unconditional: any new advisory against the candidate's inventory stops promotion until an exception or exploitability record is written. Production usually already runs the same dependency, so blocking the candidate protects nothing and can hold back an incident fix. On the day a common base image gets an advisory, every team's promotions stop. It also assumes every artefact has an inventory, which the library requires only conditionally.
findings.recommendation: Retype as SHOULD for production promotion and scope it: block only on findings above the estate's blocking threshold that the candidate introduces or worsens relative to what is running. Existing exposure goes to the remediation clock in dependencies-supply-chain.md section 2. Exempt the documented emergency path, with review afterwards.

findings.title: Invariant 8 binds only 'when policy requires it'
findings.quote: **automated abuse-case** or adversarial analysis runs as a **binding gate** (not advisory-only logs) when policy requires it
findings.critique: A rule that applies when policy requires it requires nothing. 'Automated abuse-case or adversarial analysis' names no recognisable class of check, so nobody can tell whether a pipeline has one. What is left, server-enforced with retrievable evidence, repeats invariants 1, 3 and 4. The rationale row asserts that AI-accelerated discovery rewards continuous signal and gives no source.
findings.recommendation: Remove invariant 8. Move its scope list (authentication and authorisation, secrets and cryptography, data-boundary enforcement, exposed interfaces, privileged pipeline definitions) to testing-strategy.md section 5 as the trigger for security-specific tests. Leave one sentence here: security checks claimed as merge requirements follow invariants 1, 3 and 4.

findings.title: Evidence invariant names no retention period or owner
findings.quote: retain (or stream to an organisation-controlled store) enough **evidence** to answer
findings.critique: No period, minimum or owner is given, so compliance cannot be judged. Hosted CI services delete logs and artefacts after a default window. A team can satisfy this sentence on the day of the merge and be unable to answer 'was this binary ever scanned?' at an incident review some months later, which is the case the rationale gives for having the rule.
findings.recommendation: Add: the estate records a retention period for merge and deploy evidence, no shorter than the time the artefact is deployed or supported plus its incident-review window, and exports evidence that must outlive the CI host's default retention. Add one row to checklists/build-readiness.md.

findings.title: SSDF practice groups mislabelled
findings.quote: Activities under **Protect Software (PS)** and **Produce Well-Secured Software (PO)** expect build pipelines and environments to be **hardened and verifiable**
findings.critique: PO is Prepare the Organization; Produce Well-Secured Software is PW. Two other files in this slice attribute protecting development environments and pipelines to PS, which NIST describes as protecting the software's components from tampering and unauthorised access. The cross-walk is offered to adopters as vocabulary for auditors, so the labels need to be exact.
findings.recommendation: Correct this row to name the right group for secure environments and toolchains. Check and correct merge-path section 3 row 2 and its SP 800-218 reference line, and the PS row of timeless-principles-and-tooling.md section 7, against NIST's own group descriptions; cite practice identifiers where a specific practice is relied on.

findings.title: Governed push presented as a practical equivalent of pull reconciliation
findings.quote: Reconciler **or** documented push that **replays a known revision**; no routine mystery deploys.
findings.critique: OpenGitOps principles 3 and 4 require software agents that pull desired state and continuously reconcile actual state toward it. A pipeline that applies on merge does neither: nothing observes or corrects drift between runs. Accepting governed push is a fair choice for this library, but calling it an equivalent lets a team claim conformance to the standard it does not have. The supporting citation is a vendor blog described as vendor-neutral.
findings.recommendation: Say it plainly: governed push is declarative operations, not GitOps as OpenGitOps v1.0.0 defines it. Under push, make invariant 5 concrete: a scheduled drift-detection run with an owner, since nothing else observes actual state. Remove the vendor post as the supporting source.

findings.title: Saved plans hold secrets; three files tell teams to keep them as evidence
findings.quote: apply the plan that was reviewed, or recompute it and review it again
findings.critique: Applying the reviewed plan means saving it and passing it to the apply job. The tool's publisher states that a plan file contains the full configuration and the state it applies to, and must be protected accordingly. Build section 12 and the infrastructure reference list plans as durable, retrievable evidence with no caveat. Followed literally, teams publish secret values as CI artefacts readable by anyone with repository access.
findings.recommendation: Add to invariant 7: a saved plan is sensitive. Store it encrypted with access no wider than the state itself, keep it only until apply, and retain the rendered, redacted diff as the durable evidence. Repeat the caveat in build.md section 12 and impl/infrastructure-delivery.md invariant 6.

findings.title: Drift has a third legitimate ending; reconcilers do not always self-heal
findings.quote: A reconciler does the first automatically.
findings.critique: Some fields are rightly owned by another controller: replica counts set by an autoscaler, injected sidecars, provider-computed defaults. For those the correct ending is to declare the field unmanaged, or the team fights a permanent diff. And a reconciler reverts drift only when self-healing is switched on; many run in detect-only mode, so the last sentence overstates.
findings.recommendation: Change to three endings: revert, adopt, or explicitly exclude the field from management with the owning controller named in the declaration. Reword the last sentence to 'a reconciler configured to self-heal does the first automatically'.

findings.title: Immutable-inputs invariant only raises a 'red flag'
findings.quote: using `latest` in production is a **red flag** unless policy allows it and it is **auditable**
findings.critique: An invariant that calls something a red flag unless policy allows it binds nobody. A mutable tag in production means what runs can change with no reviewed change and no new revision, which breaks invariant 2 two lines above. This is the one place the pattern addresses deployment-input immutability, and it is advice.
findings.recommendation: Retype: production desired state SHOULD reference application payloads by digest or an equivalent immutable identifier; a mutable tag is a recorded exception with owner and expiry. Evidence: no mutable tag in the production declaration.

findings.title: Entire flag lifecycle is baseline for any runtime flag
findings.quote: - Baseline: every claim below applies to any repository that evaluates a flag at runtime, whatever the flag store.
findings.critique: This line makes a five-state machine, two clocks, seven guarded transitions, human-recorded transitions with actor and reason, merge-blocking metadata and a daily stale scan mandatory for a team with three booleans in a configuration file. A small team will read the first page and ignore the whole document, including the few rules that would have helped them: owner, safe default, removal date.
findings.recommendation: Split the pattern. Baseline, about ten lines: every flag has a type, an owner, a stated safe default and a removal or review date; tests never read live flag state; stale flags are reviewed on a cadence. Move sections 3 to 5 into a 'managed rollout' profile activated for user-facing production services that use a flag service.

findings.title: Automated, metric-gated promotion is prohibited
findings.quote: Every forward change and every state transition remains human.
findings.critique: Automation may only revert. That forbids the mainstream progressive-delivery model, in which automated analysis advances exposure and halts on a breach. With the default ladder a person makes six recorded forward changes per flag per rollout. Collaboration section 8.1 places no such ban on whole-candidate canaries, so a flag change is held to a stricter rule than a deployment for no stated reason.
findings.recommendation: Allow automation to advance tiers when a human recorded the promotion criteria, guard metrics, tolerances and halt condition before the first tier, and each automated step is logged against the flag. Keep a human decision for the final step in person-affected or regulated profiles.

findings.title: Ops flag 'safe default on' is ambiguous about which way is safe
findings.quote: | Ops | Kill switch or circuit breaker | `on` (the safe state) | Operations or SRE |
findings.critique: For a kill switch, 'on' can mean the feature is enabled or the switch is engaged. Section 4.4 has automation trip an ops flag 'to its safe default', which makes the default the tripped state; the cited article's convention is that off means existing behaviour. The pattern exists so that on-call staff know which way is safe, and its own taxonomy row leaves that open.
findings.recommendation: Stop using on and off for ops flags. Define two named states, normal and tripped; say which one code falls back to when the flag store is unreachable; require the description to state the effect of tripping. Correct 'an ops switch defaulting `off`' on line 32 to match.

findings.title: Rollout numerics have no source and no sample-size floor
findings.quote: default tolerance is 1 to 2 standard deviations from baseline over the monitoring window
findings.critique: No source is given for the tier ladder, the 10 to 30 minute dwell or this tolerance, and no minimum number of observations is required. On a service handling a few requests a second, one percent for ten minutes is a handful of requests; a one-sigma band on that is noise. The gate then trips constantly or passes blind, while looking rigorous.
findings.recommendation: Replace the sigma default with a requirement that each tier observes enough traffic to detect the recorded tolerance, extending dwell until it does. Label the ladder and dwell times as illustrative, and either cite a source for them or state that there is none.

findings.title: Integration and contract suites must be parameterised by flag state
findings.quote: integration and contract tests MUST parameterise flag state
findings.critique: Parameterising every integration and contract test by flag state multiplies the suite with each concurrent flag. The article this pattern cites says it is not necessary to test every combination and that the configuration expected to go live matters most. The unit-level rule is sound; this clause prices flags out of the trunk workflow they are meant to enable.
findings.recommendation: Keep the unit-test MUST. Change the second clause to SHOULD: integration and contract suites run with the configuration expected in production and with release flags at their safe defaults; add other combinations only where flags are known to interact.

findings.title: DORA metrics framed as organisation-level; definition embellished
findings.quote: **DORA-style** metrics describe **how the organisation delivers** change
findings.critique: DORA states the metrics are meant to be applied at the application or service level, one at a time. Framing them as how the organisation delivers invites the roll-ups and cross-team comparisons that section 2.2 warns against. The table also defines deployment frequency as shipping 'safely'; DORA's definition is a count or interval of deployments. The finding that speed and stability are not trade-offs is never stated.
findings.recommendation: Reword the introduction and the rationale row: the metrics describe how one application or service, and the team owning it, delivers change. Remove 'safely' from the deployment-frequency row. Add one sentence with DORA's statement that speed and stability are not trade-offs.

findings.title: Staffing ratio, toil and onboarding targets have no source
findings.quote: a platform team of 6–10 engineers can sustain a well-scoped platform for 15–30 stream-aligned teams
findings.critique: No source supports this ratio; the cited book does not give one. Section 6 adds a target of under 20 percent toil, while the one source it cites on toil sets a 50 percent cap for a different role, and a one-day onboarding target, also unsourced. Unsourced figures in a principle get repeated in headcount and budget arguments as if they were findings.
findings.recommendation: Delete the ratio, or label it the author's heuristic with no supporting evidence. Replace the toil and onboarding figures with: set an estate target, record it, and track the trend. Apply the same treatment to 'three to five' capabilities and the quarterly cadence if they stay.

findings.title: Purpose claim ignores DORA's finding that platforms can reduce throughput and stability
findings.quote: that reduce **cognitive load** on stream-aligned teams and accelerate **safe delivery**
findings.critique: DORA's 2024 research, the library's measurement authority, reports that internal platforms improved productivity and team and organisational performance but can also lead to decreased change stability and throughput. This principle asserts faster safe delivery as the purpose and never mentions the measured downside, so a platform team is not told to look for it. Section 6 also still lists the superseded Four Keys with MTTR.
findings.recommendation: State the finding. Add: a platform SHOULD show, per consuming service, that delivery throughput and stability did not degrade after onboarding, and treat degradation as a platform defect. Replace the Four Keys line with a pointer to measurement-and-dora.md section 1; fix the same wording in checklists/release-readiness.md.

findings.title: Principle names portal products it says belong in tooling
findings.quote: - Publish golden paths through a **service catalogue or developer portal** (Backstage, Port, or equivalent).
findings.critique: The file's own introduction says product guidance for developer portals lives in tooling and this file holds portable intent; this bullet and section 7 then name two portal products and one infrastructure tool's variable format. One of the named portals is a commercial product. They are offered as examples, so the harm is small, but the layer rule is broken by the text that states it.
findings.recommendation: Replace with 'a service catalogue or developer portal' here and 'a machine-readable interface definition' in section 7. Move the product names to a tooling page.

findings.title: Metric movement said to validate the playbook
findings.quote: Improvement in deployment frequency and stability validates the playbook; doctrine text alone does not.
findings.critique: A rise in deployment frequency after adoption does not validate the playbook; team changes, product phase and tooling move the same numbers. The measurement principle warns against making delivery metrics the goal, and DORA lists that as its first pitfall. The troubleshooting table then advises selling the programme to leadership on those metrics.
findings.recommendation: Reword: sustained movement in a service's delivery metrics is consistent with the playbook working; check what else changed, and do not set the metrics as adoption targets. Change the 'Leadership wants a date' row to offer specific risk reductions, not metric values.

findings.title: Pull-request size default has no source and is high for daily integration
findings.quote: aim for **under ~400 lines** changed (insertions + deletions) **or** **under ~20 files** touched per PR
findings.critique: No source is given. The review guidance the library cites elsewhere says about 100 lines is usually reasonable and 1,000 usually too large, and that spread across files matters as much as line count. Four hundred lines is defensible as a ceiling, but it is written as the default aim, which is large for a workflow that claims frequent integration.
findings.recommendation: Present 400 lines or 20 files as the ceiling above which a change needs a stated reason, give the aim as 'reviewable in one sitting, typically 100 to 200 lines', and cite a source or say the figures are the author's default.

findings.title: Rollback authority is buried in a file about collaboration
findings.quote: ### 8.1 Deployment Canaries And Rollback
findings.critique: The rule naming who may roll back production without further approval is one of the most useful in the slice. It sits in subsection 8.1 of the collaboration principle, among summaries of flags, environments, pipelines, SLOs and observability that other files own. Nobody looking for rollback authority during an incident will open a file with this title.

findings.title: Every mandatory gate runnable locally: no carve-out where the rule is owned
findings.quote: - Every mandatory CI gate should be runnable locally with one documented command.
findings.critique: Some required gates cannot run on a laptop: the multi-platform matrix that section 9 demands, hosted code-scanning services, checks that need cloud identity, merge-queue runs. The developer-experience principle allows a documented reason for a CI-only gate, but this owner, the hooks reference and the readiness checklist state the rule without it, so a compliant repository fails its own checklist.
findings.recommendation: Type it as SHOULD and add the carve-out here: gates that cannot run locally are listed with the reason, and the local command reports which required gates it does not cover. Align impl/git-hooks.md invariant 2 and the checklist row.

findings.title: Hermetic defined as reproducible; section states no rule
findings.quote: **Hermetic** builds minimise **undeclared** inputs: lockfiles, pinned toolchains, and **reproducible** steps so the same commit yields the same artefact
findings.critique: These are different properties. A hermetic build sees only declared inputs, usually with no network access; a reproducible build gives the same output when repeated. This line defines the first by the second. The section then holds no rule: a definition, a pointer to another file, and a heading naming a framework that, as the text says, does not require hermetic builds.
findings.recommendation: Give each term one line. Retitle the section 'Declared Inputs And Provenance'. Either state one rule here (release builds SHOULD resolve only declared, pinned inputs) or delete the section and leave the subject to dependencies-supply-chain.md section 4.

findings.title: Monorepo guidance stops at 'use CODEOWNERS'
findings.quote: shared build tooling and atomic refactors; require explicit ownership boundaries (CODEOWNERS, path rules) to avoid silent coupling.
findings.critique: A monorepo's delivery problems are building and testing only what a change affects, keeping required checks meaningful when most pipelines do not run for a given change, shared-dependency version policy, and ownership of cross-cutting changes. This line and one paragraph in the build-surface pattern are the library's whole answer. A team choosing a monorepo learns nothing here about what it is taking on.
findings.recommendation: Add four conditional rules for multi-unit repositories: change-affected selection of build and test targets with a periodic full run; one aggregate required check per change; a stated policy for shared dependency versions; a named owner for changes that cross unit boundaries. Keep the neutrality on repository count.

findings.title: Host mapping omits the traps that decide whether required checks work
findings.quote: avoid listing redundant or experimental jobs as required
findings.critique: On the most common host, a required workflow skipped by a path filter stays pending and blocks the merge; a required job skipped by a condition reports success; and a merge queue runs nothing unless workflows trigger on the merge-group event. The doctrine asks for path-scoped triggers, required checks and no silent skips at once, and this page gives no way to have all three.
findings.recommendation: Add a section on skippable required checks: do not require path-filtered workflows; require one always-running aggregate job that fails unless each needed job succeeded or was deliberately not needed; trigger required workflows on the merge-group event. Mention rulesets alongside branch protection, and that administrators bypass rules unless that is switched off.

findings.title: Checklist turns an example directory into a requirement; 35 unranked rows

The checklist makes it a location rule that most ecosystems cannot meet, because the package manager fixes where its manifest lives. The list is also 35 unranked rows mixing build checks with GenAI tiering, event envelopes and a row about how this library separates tooling from principles, which no product repository can satisfy.
findings.recommendation: Reword to 'packaging metadata is tracked and reviewable, not kept in ignored output folders'. Split into a baseline of about ten rows plus conditional blocks (publishes artefacts, deploys, multi-platform). Remove the GenAI, event-envelope, message-channel and tooling-separation rows; they belong to other checklists or to none.

findings.title: New Service reference restates; only its routing table earns a place

The step table with its routes is what an engineer would use. Everything else is a second copy of each rule that must now be kept in step with its owner.

findings.title: Application Deployment reference is an index of fifteen owners

The useful core, the three inputs of a deployment declaration and the runtime shape in invariant 7, is diluted. An engineer finishes knowing which topics exist, not what a good deployment declaration contains. There is no worked example.
findings.recommendation: Keep the three-input shape, invariants 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 10, and the step table. Reduce load testing, model cost and edge runtimes to links under Boundaries. Add one product-neutral worked example of a declaration: candidate reference, bindings, bounds, labels, health signals.

findings.title: Gate versus telemetry distinction
findings.quote: A tool step that **always succeeds** while emitting warnings is **telemetry**, not a **gate**.
findings.critique: Short, testable and correct: a step that cannot fail is not a control. Together with invariant 1 (enforcement by platform configuration, not local scripts) it gives reviewers a one-question test for any claimed merge requirement. Both are implementable on any mainstream host with no special tooling.

findings.title: Cache treated as a trust boundary for release builds

findings.recommendation: Keep the strength and scope. Do not generalise it into a ban on shared caches or soften it to advice.

findings.title: Named rollback decider with bounded authority
findings.quote: can roll back to the previously verified candidate without further approval
findings.critique: Names who may act and removes the wait for permission during an incident, while limiting the authority to the previously verified candidate and requiring review afterwards. findings.title: SLO rule is an untyped universal with no scale-down
findings.quote: Typical default: 3–5 SLOs per service (or per clearly bounded user-facing product); fewer is better than many.
findings.critique: §1 reads as binding on every service, with no strength keyword, no applicability and no minimum form. A team with no SRE function cannot tell whether one SLO, or none, complies. The 3–5 figure has no source. ENGINEERING.md says objectives apply 'where appropriate'; the owner never says where.
findings.recommendation: Retype: SHOULD for production services with external users or a paging rota; MAY skip for internal tools and prototypes with the reason recorded. State the minimum form: one success-ratio SLI for the main journey, measured at the edge, over a rolling 28- or 30-day window, with a one-paragraph budget policy. Label '3–5' EXAMPLE or cite it.

findings.title: Error-budget policy is described, not required; no window, decider or triggers
findings.quote: Policy defines what happens when budget is exhausted or nearly exhausted: slow feature work, freeze risky deploys, prioritise reliability fixes
findings.critique: The sentence assumes a policy exists but never requires one or says what it contains. The cited Google example fixes a four-week window, halts non-P0 releases at exhaustion, forces a postmortem when one incident burns over 20% of budget, lists exemptions and names an escalation authority. Without those, 'budget exhausted' starts the argument the Why says a policy prevents.
findings.recommendation: SHOULD (services with SLOs): a written, product-agreed error-budget policy stating the compliance window, actions at exhaustion, who decides and who arbitrates, exemptions, and a single-incident postmortem trigger. Give a five-line small-team default. Evidence: the policy document linked from the SLO definition.

findings.title: §8 graceful stop: refusing new work on the signal still drops requests
findings.quote: On a termination signal a workload stops taking new work, finishes or returns in-flight work within the platform's grace period, and exits.
findings.critique: On the commonest orchestrator, removal from load balancing runs concurrently with the termination signal, not before it. A workload that refuses new connections the moment it is signalled rejects requests still being routed to it: the dropped-requests-on-deploy failure this section's Why claims to prevent. Separately, abrupt kill is unavoidable (out-of-memory, node loss), yet tolerance of it is only SHOULD.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: on a termination signal the workload reports not-ready, keeps serving until the platform has stopped routing to it (or a short configured delay), then drains in-flight work and exits within the grace period. Split the second sentence out as MUST for workloads holding durable state or acknowledged work: correctness does not depend on a clean shutdown.

findings.title: §8 workload runtime shape is right and at the right strength
findings.quote: Keep the checks cheap and local: a check that fails when a shared dependency is slow can remove every instance at once.
findings.critique: §8 states four runtime properties as outcomes, not as one orchestrator's features, names the failure each prevents, allows a recorded single instance, declines to mandate CPU caps where sources disagree, and discloses its evidence limits. SHOULD is the right strength for health signals, redundancy and resource declarations. Do not turn it into a product checklist or raise it wholesale to MUST.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written, subject only to the graceful-stop wording in SOPS-04.
