findings.title: Low-traffic exemption prescribes a remedy that does not fix low traffic
findings.quote: **low-traffic** services **MAY** use a single-tier alert with the reason **recorded**
findings.critique: The low-traffic problem is too few requests in the window: one failure in a quiet five minutes is a 14.4× burn. Dropping to one tier leaves that untouched and removes slow-burn detection. The cited Workbook chapter offers different remedies: synthetic traffic, aggregating services, changing the product or SLO, or lengthening windows. 'Low-traffic' is also undefined, so any service may claim it.
findings.recommendation: Replace with: where the short window holds too few requests to be meaningful (state an EXAMPLE floor), the service SHOULD use one of synthetic probes, an aggregated SLO across related services, longer windows, or a minimum-event-count guard on the alert, and record which. Keep slow-burn ticketing in every case.

findings.title: §6 burn-rate wording errors and an unstated 30-day assumption
findings.quote: Fires equally at low and high traffic; meaningless at night | Compute error ratio, then multiply by burn-rate threshold
findings.critique: The fix is mis-stated: the error ratio is compared with burn-rate threshold × budget, not multiplied by it. The row also implies burn-rate alerts behave well at night, when ratio alerts are noisiest. In §6.1, '14.4 for one hour means the budget is gone in ~2 days' merges two facts (2% in the hour; exhaustion in two days if sustained). Every threshold assumes a 30-day window, which is never stated. The table itself matches the source.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the fix cell as 'alert when the error ratio exceeds burn-rate threshold × (1 − SLO target)'. Split the §6.1 sentence in two. Add under the table: values assume a 30-day window; threshold = budget fraction × SLO window ÷ long window, and the short window is about one twelfth of the long one.

findings.title: Title-case Must/Should carry no force under the library's own rule
findings.quote: **Must** when the service has **SLOs**: each SLO has **one or more** **SLIs** with a **written** definition
findings.critique: The normative-language pattern says only capitalised keywords bind and that bold type creates no authority. Yet the SLI rule here, the saga, wait-state and human-step rules in state-machines §5, and the 'Must not' and 'must open' lines in the incident pattern use title or lower case, while their rationale tables call them mandatory. An adopter cannot tell whether these bind, and an auditor could argue either way.
findings.recommendation: Retype each line. Observability §5.1 MUST (services with SLOs); §5.2 SHOULD; §5.3 MAY. State-machines §5.1 and §5.2 MUST within their stated scope; §5.3 MUST for audited human steps. Incident pattern: decide per line between SHOULD and MUST and capitalise. Remove decorative bold from the same sentences.

findings.title: Missing 6/7: no trace sampling or telemetry retention rule
findings.quote: ## 3. Cardinality And Cost
findings.critique: Cost is governed through metric cardinality only. Trace sampling decides whether the trace for the failing request exists at all and dominates trace cost, yet the principle is silent on head versus tail sampling, keeping errors and slow requests, propagating the decision, and computing SLIs before sampling. §3 sends high-cardinality identifiers to traces and exemplars and §7 takes evidence from 'sampled production traces', so both rest on an unstated policy.
findings.recommendation: Add to §3. SHOULD (production services emitting traces): a recorded sampling policy per service or estate; errors and requests breaching the latency objective retained at a higher rate than successes; the sampling decision propagated with trace context; SLIs and rate metrics computed from unsampled data. Treat retention per signal as CONTEXT-DEPENDENT. Mechanisms stay in tooling.

findings.title: No baseline signal set for an ordinary service
findings.quote: - **Metrics** — aggregates, rates, saturation; power **SLOs** and dashboards.
findings.critique: A model call gets a seven-item MUST list; a plain HTTP or queue service gets nothing checkable. §1 describes the signals but nothing says which metrics, spans or log fields a service emits. 'Useful telemetry on material paths' cannot be verified, so the §8 post-deployment check has no expected set to check against, and the impl page can only say 'add logs, metrics, and traces'.
findings.recommendation: Add a baseline. SHOULD (production services): per inbound route template and per outbound dependency, request count, error count and a duration histogram (percentiles, not averages); saturation for each bounded resource; a span per inbound request and outbound call; logs carrying service, version, trace and span ids, and outcome. Evidence: the set visible for one sampled production request.

findings.title: Incident pattern describes incident management; an on-call engineer cannot execute it at 3 a.m.
findings.quote: Something crosses severity (§2) or a human declares an incident. Confirm impact, start the state doc (§5), assign incident command (§3).
findings.critique: Across 2,800 words there is no ordered first-fifteen-minutes sequence, no declare criteria, no rule to mitigate before diagnosing (reverse the latest change, turn the flag off), no state-document template and no default update interval. Google's chapter gives three declare triggers and says to declare early. Review triggers and deadlines are left to 'estate policy'. A paged engineer gets vocabulary, not instructions.
findings.recommendation: Open the pattern with a one-screen card: acknowledge; declare if customer-visible, a second team is needed, or unresolved after a set time; open the state doc from a template included in the pattern; name the IC; check recent changes and reverse them before diagnosing; post an update with the next update time; escalate at a stated time without progress. Add default review triggers and a drafting deadline to §9.

findings.title: Optional agent-responder section is a quarter of the incident pattern and names vendors in rule text
findings.quote: AI agents (Azure SRE Agent-class, PagerDuty virtual responder, incident.io AI SRE) rostered into incident response
findings.critique: §10 is about 670 of 2,825 words and applies only to estates rostering AI agents. It names three vendors' products in rule text and carries five vendor citations, while the human process is referenced by 'verify current URLs' and 'industry on-call practice', and §3 attributes incident command to aviation where Google's cited chapter bases it on the Incident Command System. The part most teams need is the least supported.
findings.recommendation: Move §10 to its own pattern, leaving a three-line pointer and the 'never IC' rule in §3. Keep vendor names in that pattern's references only. Cite the human process precisely: the SRE Book chapters on being on-call, managing incidents and postmortem culture, by URL. Correct the §3 Why to the Incident Command System.

findings.title: On-call sustainability has no numbers and no small-team answer
findings.quote: **Interrupt budget (conceptual):** if wakes or SEV-1s per rotation exceed a defined threshold, stop and treat as a reliability or triage program problem
findings.critique: A 'conceptual' budget against an undefined threshold binds nothing. The library gives numeric defaults for batch sizes and test ratios but none here, where its own source does: at most two incidents per 12-hour shift, on-call at most 25% of time, eight engineers for a single-site rota. Nor does it say what a team of three should do, which is the case this pattern claims to serve.
findings.recommendation: Add EXAMPLE defaults from the cited chapter and a review trigger when they are exceeded for two consecutive rotations. Add a small-team rule: SHOULD NOT promise 24×7 paging response with fewer than about five people on the rota; declare business-hours or best-effort cover, align the SLO and customer commitments to it, and record the decision.

findings.title: Chaos pattern assumes an SRE function and an unsourced cadence
findings.quote: **Frequency:** quarterly for tier-1 revenue or safety paths; after major architecture changes within 60 days
findings.critique: Quarterly and 60 days have no source, and 'tier-1' is not defined in this slice. The participant list assumes an SRE or platform facilitator and a comms observer. There is no minimum form for a team without them, so small teams will read the pattern as not for them and skip rehearsal, including the restore and dependency-loss drills other files rely on.
findings.recommendation: Label the cadence EXAMPLE and tie it to the service's availability objective. Add a minimum viable exercise: 60–90 minutes, non-production, one scenario taken from the last incident or the top critical dependency, two people, checking that the alert fired, the runbook worked and the dashboard showed it; record up to three fixes.

findings.title: Dead-lettering on an ordered stream silently corrupts per-key state
findings.quote: after N failures or specific non-retryable errors, move the message to a separate destination; do not retry forever.
findings.critique: Where consumers rely on per-key order, moving one message aside and continuing applies later events for that entity without the earlier one. Blocking instead halts the partition. The pattern presents dead-lettering as simply correct and never names the choice. It also gives no rule for delay between attempts, and requires an alert only 'before loss', not when a message arrives in the dead-letter destination.
findings.recommendation: Add: SHOULD (consumers relying on order) choose and document one of block-and-alert, park every later message for the same key, or skip and reconcile from the authoritative store. SHOULD: retries use capped exponential backoff, with count and delays recorded. SHOULD: a message entering the dead-letter destination raises a ticket-level alert to a named owner.

findings.title: A JetStream ordered consumer is not a partition analogue
findings.quote: (Kafka topic partition, JetStream ordered consumer, SQS FIFO per group)
findings.critique: An ordered consumer is a disposable single-reader cursor; NATS documentation says to use it only for reads that can restart from the top, and a named consumer with explicit ack for work that must land. It is not what an at-least-once worker uses. Ordered processing with redelivery needs explicit ack with MaxAckPending of 1; otherwise a redelivered message arrives after later ones.
findings.recommendation: Replace with 'JetStream durable consumer with explicit ack and MaxAckPending 1'. In tooling/nats-jetstream.md add three facts the page omits: publishers use JetStream publish and check the stream acknowledgement; the message-id duplicate window (two minutes by default) deduplicates publisher retries; redelivery reorders unless MaxAckPending is 1.

findings.title: Acknowledge-after-durable-effect rule is correct, typed and scoped
findings.quote: only after its effect is **durably committed**, **scheduled**, or written to an **outbox**, so a crash leads to redelivery rather than loss
findings.critique: The new acknowledgement rule is correct, typed and scoped: SHOULD by default, MUST where loss is material, and acknowledging first named as an explicit at-most-once choice that must be recorded. It agrees with the product documentation it cites on where delivery semantics come from. Later edits should add positional-commit detail in tooling, not soften the ordering or the MUST.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written. Supply the offset-commit mechanics in tooling (SOPS-44).

findings.title: Idempotency keys without atomicity or concurrency rules
findings.quote: **persist** key → outcome mapping for the documented **retry window**
findings.critique: The pattern omits what makes a key work: the deduplication record commits atomically with the effect, or the effect is conditional on it; concurrent duplicates are serialised by a unique constraint or lock; a reused key with a different payload is refused. The usual look-up-then-act implementation double-applies under exactly the race it exists for. §3 and the event-consumer page's 'look up the event identity' step repeat the gap.
findings.recommendation: Add to §§2–3. MUST (where a duplicate causes material harm): the first-outcome record and the effect commit in one transaction, or the effect is a conditional write; a second in-flight request with the same key waits or receives a conflict; a key reused with a different request is refused. SHOULD: the retention window is at least the longest client or broker redelivery horizon, and is documented.

findings.title: Idempotency §1 separates retry boundary from domain effect and refuses broker exactly-once claims
findings.quote: Do not infer business-level exactly-once behaviour from a transport or broker claim. State the duplicate and recovery invariant that the application actually enforces.
findings.critique: §1 is the best-calibrated text in the slice. It separates the retry boundary from the domain effect, does not pretend every operation is idempotent, grades SHOULD and MUST by harm, and refuses broker exactly-once marketing. Its reading of HTTP idempotent methods is accurate. Fixes elsewhere should add mechanics beneath it, not restate or dilute it.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written.

findings.title: Additive-change rule lacks a must-ignore rule and a compatibility check
findings.quote: additive changes preferred; breaking changes require a new event type or version suffix and a migration plan.
findings.critique: 'Additive preferred' sits beside 'contract violations are failures' with no rule that consumers ignore unknown fields. A consumer validating against a closed schema turns every additive change into an outage or a dead-letter flood. Nothing defines additive, says which side upgrades first, requires a compatibility check against the last published schema, or sets how long a superseded type stays published.
findings.recommendation: Add to §1. MUST (consumers): ignore unknown fields, and tolerate unknown enum values where the contract allows extension. SHOULD (producers): CI compares each schema with the last published version and fails on removal, rename, type change or new required field. SHOULD: a superseded type is published alongside its replacement for a stated window, with known consumers tracked.

findings.title: Missing 5/7: no per-entity version or sequence in state-change events
findings.quote: - Document **ordering** guarantees (per partition key, per entity, or none).
findings.critique: Documenting ordering does not let a consumer cope when it fails, and redelivery, replay, dead-lettering and repartitioning all reorder. Without a monotonic per-entity version in the payload a consumer cannot detect a stale or missing event, so projections regress silently and the reconciliation that state-machines §4 asks for has nothing to compare against.
findings.recommendation: Add to §4. SHOULD (events describing a state change of an entity): carry a per-entity monotonic version or sequence assigned at commit. Consumers apply an event only if it advances the stored version, discard older ones, and treat a gap as a signal to wait or to reconcile from the authoritative store. Occurrence time alone is not an ordering key.

findings.title: Missing 4/7: transitions are not required to be conditional writes
findings.quote: A transition is committed when durable state matches the new state and downstream effects are defined
findings.critique: §1 lists allowed transitions and §2 defines commitment, but nothing requires the store to enforce the precondition at write time. Two triggers racing from one state, such as a payment callback and a timeout job, each read the old state and both commit; the order example has exactly this pair. An allowed-transition table that the write path does not check is documentation, not a control.
findings.recommendation: Add to §2. MUST (state with concurrent triggers): a transition is written conditionally on the stored state or version still matching its precondition, in the same transaction as its outbox record; the losing trigger receives a defined outcome (no-op, retry against the new state, or compensation). Evidence: a concurrency test with two competing triggers.

findings.title: Order example defines commitment as a dual write
findings.quote: durable order row (or aggregate version) updated **and** outbound event emitted (or outboxed then published)
findings.critique: Updating a row and then emitting an event are two operations with no shared transaction: a crash between them loses the event, or publishes one for a change that rolled back. That is the failure the outbox exists to remove, and the idempotency pattern says so, yet the example presents direct emission as the main form and the outbox as a parenthesis. It is the sentence readers will copy.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: 'Committed transition = order row and outbox record written in one transaction. A relay publishes each outbox record with a stable message id, waits for the stream acknowledgement, and retries; consumers deduplicate.' Remove the direct-emit alternative, or mark it as accepting event loss.

findings.title: Order example uses Kafka header names for NATS and relies on an unreleased binary mode
findings.quote: persist the processed `ce_source` + `ce_id` pair (or idempotent DB write on order id + transition)
findings.critique: The CloudEvents NATS binding prefixes attributes `ce-`; the underscore form belongs to the Kafka binding. The same slip appears as `ce_type` here and as `ce_subject` and `ce_id` in the NATS tooling page. Binary mode exists only in the binding's 1.0.3 work-in-progress text; released v1.0.2 supports structured mode only, while the tooling baseline says 1.0 and links `main`. A team copying this is non-conformant, against event-contracts §2.
findings.recommendation: Use `ce-source`, `ce-id`, `ce-type` and `ce-subject` for NATS headers, or refer to the CloudEvents attributes `source` and `id` with no transport prefix. In tooling, pin binding links to a released tag, state that NATS binary mode is unreleased upstream, and default the example to structured mode.

findings.title: Order example offers interest retention, then promises replay
findings.quote: | Retention | `limits` or `interest` | Team choice; document RPO for replay |
findings.critique: Under interest retention JetStream deletes a message once its consumers have acknowledged it, so the time- or sequence-based replay promised in §4 is unavailable and a consumer added later sees no history. Offering it as an equal 'team choice' hides that. 'RPO for replay' misuses a recovery term for a retention window. The consumer row also omits the settings that decide ordering and redelivery timing.
findings.recommendation: State `limits` retention with an explicit maximum age sized to the replay need, and say that interest or work-queue retention gives up replay and late-joining consumers. Replace 'RPO for replay' with 'replay window'. Add ack wait, backoff and max-ack-pending to the consumer row, with the ordering consequence of each.

findings.title: Saga example has no path for failed compensation and puts the costly step first
findings.quote: | `compensating` | Undo prior steps in order | → `failed` |
findings.critique: Compensation can itself fail or hang, yet `compensating` has one exit and no dwell limit, breaking state-machines §5.2. The saga captures money before reserving stock, so its commonest failure costs a customer-visible charge and refund, after which `failed` shows the user a 'decline'. Step 3 treats a notification as compensatable. A reservation arriving after the timeout is unhandled. The example teaches the mistakes sagas are known for.
findings.recommendation: Reorder: authorise, reserve stock, capture (the point of no return), then notify as a retried step. Add `compensation_failed` leading to human review, with a dwell limit and alert on `compensating`. State that compensations are idempotent and retried until they succeed, and that a late `inventory.reserved` in a terminal state triggers a release.

findings.title: Expand/contract sequence moves readers before the backfill
findings.quote: add new structure first; move writers/readers; backfill; then remove old paths
findings.critique: As written, readers move to the new structure before it is backfilled, and so read incomplete data. The safe order is expand, write both, backfill, verify, switch readers, stop old writes, contract. The derived impl page has it right, with a verify step the owner lacks, so the reference is more correct than its authority. The neighbouring 'forward-only' bullet actually defines backward compatibility, which is a different rule.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: 'add new structure; write to old and new; backfill; verify the new shape against the old; move readers; stop writing the old; remove it in a later release, once no deployed or rollback-target version uses it.' Split the forward-only bullet into 'compatible overlap' and 'forward-only recovery'.

findings.title: Backfill batch defaults are unsourced and the top of the range is unsafe
findings.quote: 1,000–50,000 rows per batch for row-oriented OLTP, 50–500 ms pause between batches
findings.critique: A fifty-fold range is not a default. Its upper end is fifty times the default chunk of a widely used online schema-change tool (1,000 rows), and the file's own reference note disclaims support for batch-size guidance. Fixed row counts and sleeps are the wrong control: row width, indexes and replication mode decide the cost. A team copying 50,000 can stall replicas on its first backfill.
findings.recommendation: Replace with an EXAMPLE starting point of about 1,000 rows, or a batch that commits in well under a second, in its own short transaction, iterating by key range. Make feedback the rule: SHOULD pause or shrink when replica lag, lock wait or load crosses the recorded threshold. Drop the fixed pause range.

findings.title: Missing 3/7: no lock-acquisition timeout for schema change
findings.quote: (blocking locks, wide table rewrites, adding `NOT NULL` without a staged plan)
findings.critique: The principle names blocking locks but not the mechanism behind most migration outages: a quick schema statement queues behind one long transaction, and every later query on the table queues behind it. Splitting into releases does not help. Nothing requires bounding lock wait, retrying, bounding statement time, or checking for long-running transactions first. §3 asks reviewers to consider 'lock duration', which is a different control.
findings.recommendation: Add to §1. SHOULD (schema change on a table serving live traffic): run with a short lock-acquisition timeout and retry with backoff, so the change aborts instead of queueing; set a statement timeout; check for long-running transactions beforehand. Engine settings belong in tooling. Evidence: the timeout in the migration script or runner configuration.

findings.title: Missing 2/7: backups are not required to be isolated from the primary's failure and credential domain
findings.quote: - Automate backups; test restores on a cadence. An untested backup is not a control.
findings.critique: Nothing requires a backup to survive what it exists for. A copy in the same account, region and credential scope as the primary is deleted by the same compromised identity, operator mistake or regional loss. 'On a cadence' has no default and no requirement to measure achieved recovery time and data loss against the stated objectives, so the restore test cannot fail.
findings.recommendation: Add. SHOULD (data with a stated RPO): at least one copy outside the primary's credential scope and failure domain, with deletion protection or immutability for the retention period. SHOULD: restore tests at a recorded interval (EXAMPLE quarterly, and after any backup-tooling change) that record achieved RTO and RPO against target and fail when they miss.

findings.title: Rollback honesty and the maintenance-window MAY
findings.quote: document rollback as either a new forward migration or app rollback, not a fantasy “down migration” that drops data
findings.critique: The rollback honesty here is right and unusual: symmetric down migrations are the most common false comfort in schema change. The new maintenance-window MAY is also proportionate, since it keeps forward-only change, a snapshot and a stated recovery path while releasing small systems from overlap engineering. Do not reintroduce reversible-migration language or drop the MAY.
findings.recommendation: Keep both as written.

findings.title: Test-count ratios as a default that needs an ADR to leave
findings.quote: **adjust** with a short ADR or team guide if you differ
findings.critique: The source says Google 'tends to aim' for about 80/15/5 by test count and that every team's mix differs. The principle turns that into a default whose deviation needs a decision record. A count ratio predicts nothing about evidence quality, is trivially gamed with small tests, and is legitimately inverted in UI, data-pipeline and infrastructure repositories. It also contradicts the file's own evidence-first opening.
findings.recommendation: Label the table EXAMPLE and delete the ADR and 'deviations require explicit rationale' wording. State the outcome instead: a pre-merge suite fast enough to run on every change (record the time budget), end-to-end tests reserved for critical journeys, and integration coverage for every boundary the unit tests fake.

findings.title: Flaky-test rule has no detection, quarantine or retry mechanics
findings.quote: - **Flaky tests are defects** — fix, quarantine with an **owner and deadline**, or delete redundant coverage.
findings.critique: Forty-eight words cover the subject. They do not say how a flake is recognised, whether an automatic retry is allowed, what quarantine means, what deadline is reasonable, or what replaces a quarantined test on a critical path. 'Do not retry indefinitely' permits any finite retry that hides the failure. The rationale claims zero tolerance, yet no one could measure compliance.
findings.recommendation: Expand §3. SHOULD: CI records a pass-after-retry as a flake, not a pass; at most one automatic retry, always reported; quarantined tests keep running, non-blocking and visible, with an owner and an expiry (EXAMPLE two weeks) after which they are fixed or deleted; flake rate is tracked per suite; a quarantined test guarding a high-risk path needs substitute evidence before release.

findings.title: Contract-testing rule conflates three checks and gates nothing
findings.quote: validate **schemas and behaviour** with **consumer–provider contract tests** or **schema-based** checks in CI.
findings.critique: Schema validity, a breaking-change comparison with the last released contract, and verification of real consumer expectations are different checks with different owners. The rule offers them as interchangeable and does not say which side runs what, or what blocks a deploy. A team that lints its API description complies, and still ships the breaking change this section exists to stop.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite §2. SHOULD (provider): CI compares the contract with the last released version and fails on a breaking change unless the version policy allows it. SHOULD (known consumers): consumer expectations are verified against the provider build before deployment. SHOULD (consumer): tests run against provider-published fixtures, not hand-written fakes. Name the contract owner.

findings.title: Missing 7/7: no doctrine for verification in production
findings.quote: ## 4. Risk-Based Depth
findings.critique: The testing principle ends at the pipeline. Synthetic journeys, canary comparison, shadow traffic and flag-limited exposure appear only as nouns in the impl page and as one canary rule in another principle. Nothing says which claims need production evidence, or requires test traffic to be marked and kept out of billing, analytics, notifications and customer data. Teams will do it anyway, unguided.
findings.recommendation: Add a section. SHOULD (services with SLOs): a synthetic check for each critical journey, alerting like any SLI. MUST: test activity in production uses marked identities or tenants, cannot charge, notify or alter real customers, and is excluded from business metrics. Point to the canary rule in collaboration §8.1 and to telemetry verification in observability §8.

findings.title: Evidence-first opening is what lifts the testing principle above a pyramid restatement
findings.quote: It is not a universal ordering rule: exploratory work, visual design, data science, integration investigation, performance work, and legacy remediation may establish evidence differently.
findings.critique: The opening section asks for evidence able to tell success from failure, treats tests as one evidence source among several, and declines to mandate test-first ordering. The impl page's 'which claim, at which delivery surface' framing builds on it well and is more usable than its owner. Later tightening of §§1–3 should not bring back a universal technique.
findings.recommendation: Keep as written; keep the impl page's placement matrices.

findings.title: Accessibility law framed as procurement; the governing instruments are never named
findings.quote: WCAG is the de-facto benchmark; many jurisdictions reference accessible ICT for public and enterprise procurement.
findings.critique: The European Accessibility Act now reaches private-sector consumer services such as e-commerce, banking and e-books; W3C's policy listing gives its scope as public and private sector. The file names no law or harmonised standard and limits §1 to 'customer-facing or legally required', so a team cannot tell that customer-facing can mean legally required. Internal tools are excluded by construction. WCAG 2.2 AA itself is the right target and is stated accurately.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the Why and add to §0: at inception, identify the accessibility law for each market and user group and record the target. Name the main instruments as examples in References (the EU Accessibility Act with EN 301 549, the public-sector directive, national equivalents). Retype §1 as SHOULD with default WCAG 2.2 AA for any human-facing UI, internal tools included, with recorded exceptions.

findings.title: Performance budgets have no measurement, and none exist for user-perceived performance
findings.quote: - Regressions beyond budget are release blockers unless explicitly accepted with rationale.
findings.critique: A blocker with no detector never blocks. Nothing says where a regression is measured (benchmark, load test, canary comparison or production percentile), against what baseline, or over what sample. The budgets also cover only API latency and job time: neither this file nor user-facing-quality sets a budget for page load, interaction delay or layout stability on real devices.
findings.recommendation: Add: SHOULD each budget names its metric, percentile, environment, baseline and the gate that checks it (pre-merge benchmark for hot paths; canary or post-deploy comparison for services). Add to user-facing-quality: SHOULD (customer-facing web and mobile) budgets for loading, responsiveness and visual stability, from field data at a stated percentile.

findings.title: Two cost files with circular ownership: split by subject, do not merge
findings.quote: This file provides the **governance** layer those sections reference.
findings.critique: Each file points to the other for tagging. Performance-and-cost §3 is a three-bullet stub of the FinOps file; sustainability sits in the performance file while its metric is referenced from both. A reader after cost rules must read two files and reconcile them. Merging would bury performance and capacity under 2,500 words of FinOps and AI spend, so the fix is a clean split, not one file.
findings.recommendation: Rename performance-and-cost to performance and capacity; delete its §3 and move §4 sustainability into cost-and-finops or a file of its own. Make cost-and-finops the single cost owner and remove its 'complements' paragraph. Update impl and checklist links. Record in the carrying ADR that a merger was considered and why it was rejected.

findings.title: Default utilisation targets remove the failover headroom reliability §8 requires
findings.quote: CPU 60–75% at peak, memory 50–70% at peak. Sustained CPU <30% or memory <40% is a rightsizing candidate.
findings.critique: A service sized to lose one of N instances can use at most (N−1)/N of capacity at peak: 50% with two instances, 67% with three. A 60–75% peak-CPU default therefore breaks the redundancy rule for any service with fewer than four instances, and rightsizing to it converts a zone loss into an overload. The figures have no source, and an ADR is demanded to depart from them.
findings.recommendation: Replace with: for services with an availability objective, peak load must still fit after losing one failure domain, so the target is at most (N−1)/N less a burst margin; other workloads MAY run hotter. Mark any numbers EXAMPLE, cross-link reliability §8, and remove the ADR requirement for deviation.

findings.title: FinOps rules are enterprise-shaped universals with unsourced thresholds
findings.quote: `environment` (prod/staging/dev), `owner-team`, `cost-centre`, `application`, and `product`
findings.critique: Five mandatory tags, 85% and 90% allocation targets, daily scans, 'non-negotiable' showback and a FinOps practice coordinating finance are written as untyped imperatives for everyone. A single team on one account needs a budget, an anomaly alert and an owner. The thresholds (85/90/10%, £5k per resource, 15% week-on-week, 10% over forecast) have no source and one is in a single currency. 'FinOps Foundation research shows' cites nothing.
findings.recommendation: Add an applicability paragraph. Baseline for any paid cloud use (SHOULD): a budget with alerting, a spend-anomaly alert and a named owner. Allocation, showback and unit-economics rules SHOULD apply once spend is shared across teams or cost centres. Mark every threshold EXAMPLE, remove the currency, and cite or delete the research claim.

findings.title: Agent-payment and AI-evaluation material crowds two general principles
findings.quote: **Standards watch** *(informative, not normative — items are announced, preview, or vendor-specific
findings.critique: About 39% of the cost principle is AI spend and agent payment authority; §7.1 is an authorisation control, not cost management, and ends in a paragraph of four vendors' press releases and an undefined 'ledger'. In testing-strategy, one 203-word bullet on agent-hijack evaluation outweighs the flaky-test and contract-test sections combined. Readers seeking the core subject wade through material that applies to few systems and dates quickly.
findings.recommendation: Move cost §7.1 to the agent identity and authority doctrine, leaving a pointer; move the standards-watch paragraph to an evolution note; define or remove 'ledger'. Move the adaptive-evaluation bullet in testing §5 to the agent-security pattern it already cites, leaving one sentence. No rule changes strength.

findings.title: Burn-rate example omits the 6× page tier and adds duration clauses the source rejects
findings.quote: **Author a rule for every window the alerts query** — all four below
findings.critique: The principle's table has three tiers and tells readers to use all three, yet the example has no 30-minute recording rule and no 6× alert. Copied as written, a sustained 6× burn (5% of budget every six hours) never pages. The alerts also add `for: 2m` and `for: 1h`; the cited Workbook chapter says it does not recommend duration clauses for SLO alerts, and its final rules use none.
findings.recommendation: Add the `rate30m` recording rule and make the page alert `(1h and 5m above 14.4×) or (6h and 30m above 6×)`, as in the Workbook. Remove both `for:` clauses, or keep at most a very short one on the page alert with the reason stated. Say 'five windows'. Note that the thresholds assume a 30-day SLO window.

findings.title: Kafka page gives no commit mechanics; default auto-commit undermines its at-least-once claim
findings.quote: Position in a partition; **committed** offsets define **at-least-once** progress.
findings.critique: Committed offsets give at-least-once only when committed after processing. Kafka's default is automatic commit every five seconds, which can commit records handed to other threads before they finish. The acknowledgement rule sends readers to tooling for mechanics, and this page has none: nothing on disabling auto-commit, committing the lowest completed offset under concurrency, rebalances, the poll-interval limit, dead-lettering by plain consumers, or share groups.
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Acknowledgement mapping' section: disable auto-commit or process synchronously inside the poll loop; commit only up to the lowest contiguous completed offset; commit on partition revocation; keep processing inside the poll-interval limit; a new group id starts at the reset policy (default latest, which skips backlog); the application publishes to the dead-letter topic before committing. Mention share groups as the queue-style alternative.

findings.title: Service Observability page restates categories; an engineer cannot act on it
findings.quote: | Instrument | Add logs, metrics, and traces to the main path, with structured logs. |
findings.critique: The step table says to add logs, metrics and traces, correlate them and keep labels low: the owner's headings in table form. It does not say which metrics, which spans, what a log line carries, or how to confirm arrival. About a third of the page is model-call and audit conditionals. The cause is upstream: with no baseline signal set in the owner, the page has nothing concrete to compose.
findings.recommendation: After the owner gains a baseline (SOPS-10), rewrite the step table with a concrete output per step: counter and duration histogram per route and dependency, a span per inbound and outbound call, required log fields, and the query that proves arrival after deploy. Move the model-call and audit variations below a short core, or into their own references.

findings.title: Registry precedence is the dependency-confusion pattern, not its fix
findings.quote: configure package managers to resolve internal packages from the private registry **first**
findings.critique: Precedence is the mechanism dependency confusion exploits: several resolvers take the highest version across all configured sources, so 'private first' is not a setting that exists or holds everywhere. Line 99 has a related gap: a scope protects only if the organisation owns it on the public registry. The quoted `poetry install --no-update` is not a Poetry command, and `go mod verify` checks the module cache, not lockfile drift.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: internal names resolve only from the private source, through explicit name- or namespace-to-source mapping or a single proxy that refuses public resolution for internal namespaces; no multi-source fallback. Add: claim the organisation's scope or namespace on the public registries it uses. Replace the command list with one portable sentence (install from the committed lock and fail on drift) and move per-tool commands to tooling/, corrected (`poetry check --lock`, `go mod tidy -diff`). Fix the same command in the rationale table (line 139).
findings.external_basis: https://python-poetry.org/docs/cli/ (no --no-update option on install); resolver behaviour from knowledge, not checked

findings.title: No release-age delay before bot updates merge
findings.quote: Updates that estate policy classifies as **low risk** MAY merge through a **documented bot-only path**
findings.critique: A bot path that merges fresh releases once checks pass is how compromised versions spread: checks cannot recognise a malicious release published an hour ago, and the attacker chooses the version number. Both update bots the library names now ship a release-age delay for this reason. The principle has no such rule, and install scripts are restricted only inside the clause about AI-proposed packages.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 2: SHOULD (all version updates; security fixes exempt but human-reviewed): wait a minimum release age before a bot opens or merges an update (EXAMPLE: 3 to 14 days). MUST NOT auto-merge an update younger than that age. Add to section 7 as a general rule, not an agent-only one: dependency install scripts are disabled by default in CI, with a reviewed allowlist. In section 4, pair digest pinning with bot-managed digest bumps so that pins do not freeze unpatched base images, and replace 'verify digest before pull' with verifying the base image's signature or provenance where the publisher provides one.

findings.title: SBOM MUST requires attaching, which the cited regimes do not
findings.quote: produce a machine-readable **SBOM** (Software Bill of Materials) at build time and attach it to the artefact.
findings.critique: Generating and retaining an SBOM for anything shipped externally is defensible. Requiring it to be attached to the artefact is not what the cited regimes ask: the Cyber Resilience Act has manufacturers draw one up for technical documentation and does not oblige publication. A MUST to distribute the component inventory with every external artefact, including open-source releases, is stronger than its evidence. Hosted services ship no artefact at all.
findings.recommendation: Split the rule. MUST (trigger set): generate at build time and retain an SBOM bound to the artefact digest. Delivery or publication to recipients: MUST only where law or contract demands it, MAY otherwise. State how the trigger applies to hosted services (the deployed image is the artefact; retention only). In the rationale, drop 'increasingly' for the US federal case: the governance pattern in this library already cites OMB M-26-05 as making these materials optional for agencies.
findings.external_basis: from knowledge, not checked (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 recital 77 and Annex I Part II(1); the EUR-Lex page returned no text when fetched)

findings.title: A tenant-signed attestation is presented as SLSA provenance
findings.quote: attach to the artefact via `cosign attest` or the SLSA GitHub generator action
findings.critique: SLSA Build L2 requires provenance generated by the build platform's control plane, not by a tenant. A predicate assembled and signed with `cosign attest` in a user-defined step is tenant-generated, so the mechanism this bullet prescribes does not reach the L2 target that line 56 sets. It is also an untyped imperative naming two products in a principle. Line 56 separately gives one externally shipped artefact two targets, L2 and L3.
findings.recommendation: Replace with: use the build platform's own provenance generation and confirm the level the platform documents; provenance written or signed by user-defined build steps is Build L1 evidence at most. Move the cosign and generator names to tooling/. On line 56 make the triggers disjoint: L2 for the trigger set; L3 where one build compromise would reach many downstream consumers or an active profile demands it; delete 'customer-facing'.

findings.title: Signing rule is Sigstore-for-containers stated as the general case
findings.quote: sign them using **cosign** with keyless signing via OIDC
findings.critique: The rule is written for container images on public Sigstore and applied to all 'release binaries'. Those usually need the distribution channel's own scheme: operating-system code signing with hardware-held certificates, PGP for some package repositories, registry-native attestations. For them 'no long-lived signing keys' is unachievable. A public transparency log also discloses repository and workflow identities, which private estates should decide deliberately. Public Fulcio's documented issuers do not include Azure DevOps.
findings.recommendation: Retitle the section 'Artefact Signing And Verification'. State the capability: sign with the mechanism the distribution channel and its verifiers require; use identity-based short-lived signing where the channel supports it; where it requires a long-lived key, hold the key in an HSM or KMS as a registered fallback under zero trust section 2. Add: decide whether signing metadata may go to a public transparency log. Keep the verify-against-identity rule unchanged. Move cosign, Fulcio, Rekor and CI product names to tooling/ and drop the Azure DevOps example.
findings.external_basis: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/fulcio/main/docs/oidc.md (issuer list); code-signing and registry signing requirements from knowledge, not checked

findings.title: Example patch targets are unsourced, CVSS-keyed and faster than CISA's
findings.quote: | **Critical** (e.g. network RCE, trivial auth bypass, wormable) | **24 hours** |
findings.critique: The example targets cite no source and are keyed to CVSS labels. Twenty-four hours to a patched release for every critical-rated component is faster than CISA's current federal directive, which replaced severity labels with timelines conditioned on exposure, known exploitation, automatability and impact, and sets three days for the worst combination. The lifecycle principle tells estates to publish one such table; a team that adopts this one will breach it routinely.
findings.recommendation: Keep the table illustrative but rebuild it: (1) a decision clock (triage and a named owner within one working day for known-exploited or internet-exposed findings); (2) remediation targets keyed to exposure, known exploitation and reachability, not to the CVSS label alone; (3) components with a recorded not-affected status excluded. Cite the benchmark used. Add the small-team form: known-exploited and exposed first, everything else on the regular update cadence.

findings.title: Model-format MUST recognises only pickle and tensor-only files
findings.quote: Production model loading MUST use **non-executable weight formats** (**safetensors**-class: tensor data only, no deserialization hooks).
findings.critique: The MUST recognises two kinds of artefact: pickle and 'tensor data only'. Mainstream serving formats that carry a computation graph (ONNX, SavedModel, TorchScript, Keras archives) are neither, so a team serving them cannot tell whether it complies or needs an exception. Line 116 has a similar problem: it requires a transparency-log entry and Sigstore keyless verification although the cited signing specification is PKI-agnostic and the publisher chooses the trust root.
findings.recommendation: State the property, not the format: loading MUST NOT execute code or arbitrary operators supplied by the artefact. Tensor-only formats satisfy it; graph formats are admitted with recorded loader restrictions (no custom operators or lambda layers, safe-mode loading); pickle-class keeps the sandbox-plus-exception path. Line 116: verify against the publisher's documented identity and trust root, plus log inclusion where the signature is a Sigstore bundle. Line 119: ML-BOM arrived in CycloneDX 1.5, not 1.6.
findings.external_basis: from knowledge, not checked (format behaviour; the CycloneDX 1.5 date was seen only in a search summary of cyclonedx.org/news/cyclonedx-v1.5-released/)

findings.title: Untrusted pipeline triggers and unpinned third-party steps have no owner rule
findings.quote: **Cache trust:** release and deploy builds restore only caches written at the same or higher trust
findings.critique: The incident this section cites began with a workflow that ran fork code with repository privileges and wrote a cache the release job later restored. The owner text has the cache rule but not the two controls that come before it: jobs triggered by untrusted contributions get no secrets, write token, federated identity or shared writable cache, and third-party pipeline steps are pinned to immutable references. Both appear today only as tooling tips.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 4, or to the pipeline-integrity owner with a pointer here: SHOULD, and MUST for pipelines holding publish or deploy authority: (a) jobs triggered by unreviewed contributions run without secrets, write-scoped tokens, federated identity or writable shared caches; (b) third-party actions, plugins and build images are referenced by commit hash or digest and updated through the same reviewed path as dependencies. Evidence: the pipeline configuration and a negative test from a fork.

findings.title: Secretless MUST tests only the target and has no brownfield path
findings.quote: where the target accepts federated or platform-issued workload identity, authenticate with that short-lived, audience-scoped credential
findings.critique: The MUST fires whenever the target can federate, whether or not the workload's own platform can issue a verifiable identity. An on-premises or legacy workload calling a cloud API therefore needs an exception, not a registered fallback, because the target 'accepts' federation. Every existing stored secret for a federatable target also needs its own ten-field exception from day one: hundreds of records in a brownfield estate, with no migration mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Condition the MUST on both ends: the workload's platform can issue a verifiable identity and the target accepts it. Where the source cannot, the secret is a registered fallback with that reason. For existing estates allow one time-boxed migration record per platform that lists the in-scope secrets, orders them by blast radius and carries an end date; individual exceptions start only after that date. Give 'recheck' on line 22 a trigger: at each rotation and at least yearly, with the last rotation date held in the register.

findings.title: No rule on the federation trust policy that secretless access depends on
findings.quote: Prefer **short-lived**, **audience-scoped** credentials issued to workloads
findings.critique: Secretless access moves the risk from the stored key to the trust policy, and the principle says nothing about it. The usual finding in a federated estate is a relying-party policy with a wildcard subject or no audience condition, so any repository, branch, fork or namespace can assume the production role. 'Short-lived' has no bound, so compliance cannot be judged.
findings.recommendation: Add MUST (same scope as the secretless default): the relying party binds trust to one issuer, an exact audience and specific subject claims (repository and protected ref or environment; cluster, namespace and service account); no wildcard subjects on roles with production or publish authority. Evidence: the policy text and a negative test showing an unintended identity is refused. State an EXAMPLE lifetime bound, for instance one hour or less for pipeline tokens. Mirror both in the implementation reference's Federate and Verify steps.

findings.title: Human access rule is hedged and names no evidence
findings.quote: **Human** access to production uses **MFA** and **just-in-time** elevation where the estate supports it.
findings.critique: 'Where the estate supports it' can be read as qualifying MFA as well as just-in-time elevation, so the sentence binds nothing. Phishing-resistant authentication appears only in a threat-landscape note in another file. Break-glass 'rare, monitored, reviewed' names no evidence. There is no access review or leaver revocation. An auditor asks for all four on the first day.
findings.recommendation: Retype: MUST: multi-factor authentication for all human access to production and to privileged tooling (source-control administration, CI, cloud consoles, secret stores). SHOULD: phishing-resistant factors for privileged roles. SHOULD: just-in-time elevation. Break-glass: every use alerts, is reviewed within a stated time, and the credential is rotated afterwards; the path is tested on a cadence. Add: privileged access is reviewed periodically and revoked on role change or departure.

findings.title: No leaked-secret response rule in the owner
findings.quote: lists names and shape, not values; real secrets never committed.
findings.critique: The owner says secrets are never committed but not what happens when one is. The only statement of the response in the library sits in a git-hooks implementation page, which is not allowed to own rules. Rotation 'on a cadence' has no example bound, and common leak surfaces (infrastructure state files, image layers and build arguments, crash dumps, tickets and chat) are not named.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 4 or section 2: MUST: a secret that reached a shared remote, log, ticket, image, state file or chat is treated as compromised: revoke or rotate first, review its use, then clean up; removing it from history is not remediation. SHOULD: scan at push time and across history. Name the leak surfaces above. Give an EXAMPLE maximum age for registered fallback secrets so that 'cadence' can be checked.

findings.title: OWASP table claims controls the body does not contain
findings.quote: | **API2** | Broken authentication | §2–3; strong session/token handling; rate limits on auth paths |
findings.critique: The cross-reference table promises controls the body does not contain. Section 2 is two bullets. Token and session handling, writable-field allowlists, per-route role checks and step-up for sensitive flows exist only as table cells; response-side property filtering and tenant isolation appear nowhere. The three highest-ranked API risks get less text than GraphQL depth limits, and the Service API reference states the allowlist rule more firmly than its owner does.
findings.recommendation: Expand section 2 into typed rules. MUST: authorisation is enforced server-side and deny-by-default for every object, function and property; the tenant and subject come from the authenticated principal, never from request parameters; request binding uses an allowlist and responses return only fields the caller may read. MUST: tokens are validated for signature, issuer, audience, expiry and an algorithm allowlist. SHOULD: each route has a negative authorisation test. Add step-up and automated-abuse detection for sensitive business flows to section 3.
findings.external_basis: https://owasp.org/www-project-api-security/ (2023 is still the current edition); category content from knowledge, not checked

findings.title: No transport-security rule and no default cryptographic profile
findings.quote: A portable principle does not freeze one short algorithm menu for every platform and jurisdiction.
findings.critique: No rule in this principle requires encrypted transport. TLS appears once, as a description of what public APIs 'typically' use. Section 2.1 then defers every cryptographic choice to a 'maintained profile' that the library does not supply and a small team does not have, so for them the section binds nothing. A baseline that covers post-quantum agility but not TLS has its priorities inverted.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 2.1: MUST: all traffic crossing a trust boundary uses TLS with certificate validation; plaintext listeners refuse or redirect. SHOULD: browser-facing hosts send HSTS. Add a fallback: where no profile is active, the estate's default profile is the platform's current secure defaults plus the cited OWASP cheat sheets for protocol versions, password storage and key handling. This names no algorithm and still gives a solo developer something to check.

findings.title: No input-handling, request-forgery or resolution-time SSRF rule
findings.quote: Use this table in reviews and threat modeling so no category is silently ignored.
findings.critique: The principle follows the OWASP API list category by category, and that list has no injection entry. So the library has no rule on validating input against the contract, building queries and commands safely, unsafe deserialisation or file upload, and never mentions cross-site request forgery for cookie-authenticated endpoints. The SSRF section filters by address string and omits resolution-time checks. A penetration tester starts with exactly these.
findings.recommendation: Add a section 'Input Handling'. MUST: requests are validated against the contract at the boundary and unknown fields or wrong types are rejected; queries and commands use parameterised interfaces, never string assembly; untrusted data is not deserialised into executable types. SHOULD: uploads are size-, type- and content-checked and stored outside the execution path. In section 6 add request-forgery protection for cookie-authenticated routes. In section 8 validate the resolved address at connection time, cover IPv6 and mapped ranges, and re-check on every redirect.

findings.title: CORS rule warns about the case browsers already block
findings.quote: treat `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` paired with credentials as a code smell
findings.critique: Browsers refuse a credentialed request when the response carries a wildcard origin, so the configuration warned about cannot leak data. The exploitable mistake is different: reflecting the request's Origin header, or allowing the null origin, together with credentials. The text warns about the harmless case and misses the dangerous one.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: when credentials are allowed, the allowed origin comes from a server-side allowlist of exact origins; never reflect the request Origin and never allow `null`. A wildcard is acceptable only for unauthenticated public resources. Send `Vary: Origin` where the header value depends on the request.

findings.title: Cryptographic inventory is sound but misplaced and has no small-team form
findings.quote: which data must stay confidential beyond the transition horizon
findings.critique: The inventory and agility rules are sound at SHOULD and not premature: every published transition plan starts with discovery. Three problems remain. They sit in an API-boundary file although they apply to all cryptography, so few readers will find them. There is no small-team form. 'Transition horizon' is undefined when no profile is active and no evidence form is named, so compliance cannot be judged.
findings.recommendation: Move sections 2.1 and 2.2 to their own principle or to the secure development lifecycle and leave a pointer. Add a scale-down sentence: where all cryptography is provider-managed transport and key management, the inventory is that list plus the provider's published roadmap. Define the horizon by reference to the active profile and say what applies when none is active. Name the evidence: a dated inventory record with an owner and a review trigger.
findings.external_basis: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2026/NIST.IR.8547.pdf (the section's 2030 and 2035 statement matches the final report)

findings.title: Nobody can tell whether a threat model is required
findings.quote: New internet-exposed API, auth flow, data store, or message topology.
findings.critique: Neither this file nor the lifecycle principle that points to it carries a strength keyword, so a team cannot tell whether a threat model is required before an internet-facing launch or merely suggested. 'Revisit after major changes' names no trigger, owner or evidence. The one firm instruction, recording 'not in scope', falls on the lowest-risk systems.
findings.recommendation: Type it. SHOULD (new or materially changed trust boundary), and MUST where estate policy or an active profile says so and for internet-exposed systems holding personal or regulated data: a dated threat model exists before first production exposure and is updated when a trust boundary, identity model or data class changes. Evidence: the artefact linked from the design record, with open risks owned and dated. Drop the 'not in scope' record for local, single-owner tools.

findings.title: A STRIDE walk alone omits ranking, abuse, privacy and actors
findings.quote: walk STRIDE (below) and capture threat → mitigation → residual risk in a short table or ADR subsection
findings.critique: As the only threat-modelling guidance, a STRIDE walk leaves four gaps. Threats are not ranked, so there is no way to decide what to fix first. Abuse of intended function (fraud, scraping, automation of business flows) fits no letter. Privacy harm is absent although the privacy principle requires impact assessment. Actors and assets are never listed, and detection is not offered as a mitigation class.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 2: list assets and actors (external, tenant, insider, supplier, compromised pipeline) before the walk; rank each threat on a simple likelihood-and-impact scale and order work by it; each accepted mitigation names the test or detection that shows it holds. Add two prompt rows to section 3: 'Abuse of intended function' and 'Privacy harm (linking, identifying, over-collection)', the second linking to privacy section 5.1. Add a time-box and participants line. Cut section 3.2 from two long paragraphs to a prompt table with links.

findings.title: GDPR-derived duties stated as universal, in an undefined strength
findings.quote: **Must:** when processing is likely to result in **high risk** to individuals
findings.critique: Sections 5.1 to 5.3 state duties drawn from the GDPR as universal, in a title-case 'Must' that the library's own rules say carries no defined strength. Section 5.4 gates a comparable EU duty behind a registered profile. A team outside GDPR scope cannot tell whether an impact assessment is doctrine or foreign law. The trigger list also loosens the statute, which says large-scale systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas.
findings.recommendation: Pick one model for all four subsections. Recommended: state the engineering practice as library policy with capitalised keywords (SHOULD: assess privacy impact before go-live when processing is likely to put individuals at high risk; MUST where an active privacy profile requires it) and move the legal trigger lists and consent conditions to the profile, as section 5.4 does. In section 5.3 replace the SP 800-218A mapping, which is a secure-development profile for model builders, with the NIST Privacy Framework.

findings.title: Personal-data breach notification is absent
findings.quote: ## 6. Contractual And Regulated Data Profiles
findings.critique: The library added profile-gated reporting clocks this week, with a product-security regulation as the worked example. The clock most adopters are actually under, notifying a supervisory authority of a personal-data breach within 72 hours of becoming aware, is not mentioned in the privacy principle, and incident triage is never told to ask whether personal data is affected.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 6, or as a new section 'Personal-Data Incidents': SHOULD: incident triage asks early whether personal data is affected and records when the estate became aware; where a privacy regime is in scope, its notification duties are registered as reporting obligations in the profile and exercised under secure development lifecycle section 3.1. Give the GDPR Art 33 and Art 34 duties as a second worked example beside the existing one.

findings.title: No data inventory rule and no rule on personal data outside production
findings.quote: **Retention periods** are explicit per data category (account data, logs, analytics, backups).
findings.critique: Retention 'per data category' presumes the team knows what personal data it holds and where, but no rule asks for that record; the platform checklist demands a 'PII inventory' that has no owner. Nothing covers copying production personal data into test or development environments, the commonest way minimisation fails in practice. Individual rights other than erasure are not addressed, and erasure does not mention backups.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 1: SHOULD (systems holding personal data): keep a record of which personal-data categories are held, where, for what purpose and for how long, updated when a schema or data flow changes. Add: MUST NOT copy production personal data into non-production environments unless it is masked or the environment carries production-grade access control and retention. Extend section 2: access and export requests have a tested path, and erasure states how backups age out.

findings.title: A durable principle carries a deadline that expires in two weeks
findings.quote: providers of systems already on the market before that date have until **2026-12-02** for the Art 50(2) marking duty
findings.critique: A principle described as durable carries a transitional deadline that passes two weeks after today, an amending regulation's number, fine amounts and guidance publication dates, while saying the profile, not this file, carries the applicability decision. The bullet is stale on 3 December. On line 75, 'harm-surface evidence where the AI inventory points' is private vocabulary for 'tested before launch and recorded'.
findings.recommendation: Keep the article-by-article duty summary. Move application dates, the transitional deadline, the amending regulation, fine levels and guidance dates into a worked profile example or the ADR, where a dated review trigger already exists. Rewrite line 75 in plain words: disclosures are tested before launch and the result is recorded against the system's inventory entry.
findings.external_basis: the amendment and the 2026-12-02 date were confirmed only through secondary legal summaries found by search; EUR-Lex was not loaded

findings.title: Audit integrity rule protects against the application only
findings.quote: Treat audit streams as **append-only** from the application’s perspective.
findings.critique: 'Append-only from the application's perspective' protects against the application and nobody else. The people an audit trail exists to hold to account are administrators, and nothing here keeps records out of their reach, detects deletion or moves records off the producing system. 'Proportionate' with no floor means an auditor cannot fail any design. The file contains no capitalised keyword at all.
findings.recommendation: Add MUST (in-scope audit events): records leave the producing system promptly for a store that the producing system's operators and service identities cannot alter or delete; attempts to alter, delete or disable audit collection are themselves recorded and alerted. SHOULD: tamper evidence (object lock or hash chaining) where records support legal or regulatory evidence. Evidence: the store's permissions and a test deletion that is refused and alerted.

findings.title: No clock synchronisation, failure behaviour or origin fields
findings.quote: **When** — UTC timestamp with agreed precision.
findings.critique: Timestamps are required but clock synchronisation is not, so cross-system timelines cannot be trusted. Nothing says what happens when the audit write fails: block the action, queue it, or drop the record silently. The field list omits where the event happened and where it came from (system, environment, source address or workload), an event type, and the before and after reference for permission and configuration changes.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 2: source and origin, system and environment, event type from a controlled list, and a before/after reference for configuration and permission changes. Add: SHOULD: sources synchronise to an authoritative time source and record both event time and ingest time. MUST: each event class has a stated failure behaviour (privileged actions fail closed or queue durably), and gaps in the audit pipeline alert. SHOULD: untrusted values are encoded so they cannot forge entries.

findings.title: Retention has no floor; no baseline event set or review duty
findings.quote: **Retention** per legal and product policy; **shorter** than cold storage backups where regulation requires minimisation.
findings.critique: The retention rule is one unclear sentence with no floor: it is not evident what 'shorter than cold storage backups' requires. There is no minimum event set, so two teams following the principle can record entirely different things, and no duty for anyone to review or alert on the records. No checklist in the library prompts for audit logging at all.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: each audit record class has a documented retention period with its legal or policy basis, a searchable window and an archive window (EXAMPLE: twelve months retained, three searchable), and backups holding audit records expire on the same schedule. Add a baseline event list: authentication success and failure, authorisation denial, privilege and policy change, administrative action, bulk export, key and secret operations, audit configuration change and audit-log access. Name a review or alerting owner. Add a platform-readiness checklist line.
findings.external_basis: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html (event list); the retention example is from knowledge, not checked

findings.title: Pod security rule names no Pod Security Standards level
findings.quote: align with current Kubernetes Pod Security mechanisms for your version
findings.critique: Kubernetes publishes three named Pod Security Standards levels and ships an admission controller that enforces them. The principle names neither and hedges with 'for your version'. 'Restrict privileged pods' cannot be checked: nobody can say which level a namespace must meet or what an exemption looks like.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: SHOULD, and MUST for multi-tenant or internet-facing clusters: enforce the Baseline level cluster-wide and the Restricted level for application namespaces, through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine; exemptions are per namespace, recorded and owned; use warn and audit modes before enforce when migrating. Evidence: namespace labels or policy bindings, and a privileged pod that admission refuses.

findings.title: Network-policy rule misses intra-namespace traffic, egress and enforcement
findings.quote: default deny between namespaces unless explicitly allowed; ingress/egress documented
findings.critique: Two omissions. 'Between namespaces' leaves pods inside a namespace open to each other and sets no clear rule for egress, which is how a compromised pod reaches the metadata service and the internet. And a NetworkPolicy has no effect unless the cluster's network plugin enforces it; the API accepts the object regardless, so a team can comply on paper with nothing enforced.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite: SHOULD: every application namespace has a default-deny policy selecting all pods for both ingress and egress, with explicit allows (including DNS); egress to node and cloud metadata addresses is denied unless required. MUST: confirm that the network plugin enforces policies, with a connectivity test that fails once the policy is applied. Evidence: the policies and the test result.

findings.title: Kubernetes page is too thin to serve as a baseline
findings.quote: Audit logs for API server actions where the cloud or platform provides them (enable per vendor guidance).
findings.critique: The page is about a dozen untyped bullets and is not a usable baseline. It omits per-pod workload identity and blocking node credentials, service-account token mounting, single sign-on for humans in place of long-lived client certificates, API endpoint exposure, version and patch currency, admission fail-open behaviour and limits on reading Secrets. API audit logging is hedged, and justified as a debugging aid instead of detection and forensic evidence.
findings.recommendation: Either expand the page into a typed baseline keyed to the sections of the hardening guide it already cites and a benchmark (identity and access, workload isolation, network, secrets, supply chain, audit, upgrades), or cut it to scope plus pointers to those sources. In either case retype line 39: MUST (production clusters): API server audit logging is enabled and shipped off-cluster. In section 1 put workload identity first and note that synchronising operators still create Secret objects in etcd, so encryption at rest and tight read access remain necessary.

findings.title: Timestamp is not bound into the signature; comparison rule missing
findings.quote: Require a timestamp or monotonic event id from the sender; reject events outside a short clock-skew window (for example 5 minutes)
findings.critique: The freshness check is sound only if the timestamp is inside the signed content; otherwise an attacker replays a captured body with a new timestamp. The pattern does not say so. It also omits constant-time signature comparison, verifying before parsing, and what to do when a provider offers no signature. A community specification now covers these points and is not cited.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 1: the signed content includes the delivery identifier and timestamp with the raw body; compare signatures with a constant-time function; verify before parsing the body. Add: where a provider cannot sign, use a per-endpoint secret, mutual TLS, or fetch the event back from the provider's API by identifier before acting on it. Cite the Standard Webhooks specification as the default shape for senders and receivers.

findings.title: SSDF 'Protect' practice group is misdescribed
findings.quote: | **PS — Protect** | Harden environments, tools, and pipelines against tampering |
findings.critique: The table's stated purpose is to give assessors a mapping, and this row maps wrongly. In the framework PS is 'Protect the Software': protect code and releases from tampering and unauthorised access and let consumers verify release integrity. Hardening development environments and toolchains belongs to Prepare the Organization. The rationale under section 2 stretches PS to build pipelines in the same way.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the row: 'PS, Protect the Software: protect code and releases from tampering and unauthorised access; provide release-integrity verification; archive releases', linking to dependencies sections 4 and 5 and merge-path evidence. Move environment and pipeline hardening to the PO row. Correct the section 2 rationale to match.

findings.title: No rule to publish a vulnerability reporting channel; rest is thin
findings.quote: prepare fixes or mitigations before public detail when possible; credit researchers per policy.
findings.critique: Outside section 3 the principle is five untyped bullets. It names no security verification beyond static and dependency analysis, and its training rule ('engineers know where expectations live') cannot be checked. Coordinated disclosure covers what to do with a report but not how one arrives: there is no rule to publish a reporting contact or policy, the first thing a researcher or a product-security regulator looks for.
findings.recommendation: Add to section 3: SHOULD, and MUST for products shipped to external parties: publish a vulnerability reporting contact and policy (a security contact file or repository security policy), acknowledge reports within a stated time, track them to closure and publish advisories with identifiers. State that first-party findings from testing use the same response targets as dependency findings. Replace section 4 with an observable item: security-sensitive change classes are named in the review template and onboarding covers them.

findings.title: Profile-gating has no duty to ask whether a regime applies
findings.quote: **Applicability precedes mapping.** Record the law, regulation, contract clause, customer term, or approved estate decision that makes the profile relevant.
findings.critique: Four principles now say a legal duty is not universal doctrine until someone registers a profile. Law applies whether or not anyone registers anything, and nothing in the library obliges anyone to ask the question. A team that never screens for applicability complies fully with the doctrine and may be in breach of statute. As written, profile-gating lets the library avoid stating duties without ensuring they are found.
findings.recommendation: Add a rule ahead of invariant 1: SHOULD (every production system), and MUST where the estate sells into regulated markets or handles personal data: a named owner records an applicability screen (markets and jurisdictions, data classes, product type, customer terms) at service creation and when any of those change. The outcome is either 'no external profile', dated and owned, or a registered profile. Offer a non-normative prompt list of commonly binding regimes and link the screen from the new-service reference.

findings.title: Pattern is shaped by one contractual baseline and has no small form
findings.quote: The worked profile is NIST SP 800-171 for Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI).
findings.critique: The record, the selection table and the assessment semantics are shaped by one US contractual baseline: markings, organisation-defined parameters, a paired assessment publication. The duties other principles now route here are statutes with roles, article sets and reporting clocks, which those fields do not fit. A five-person team told to register an EU AI Act profile has no example of one, and an eleven-field record is out of proportion to a disclosure banner.
findings.recommendation: Split the pattern. Keep a generic core that any regime fits on one page: authority and version (including amendments), the estate's role, scope, obligation list, evidence, reporting clocks, owner and review trigger. Move section 4 and the CUI-specific fields to an annex example. Add a second worked example for a statute that a principle already references, and state the minimum form for a small team.

findings.title: DFARS example omits the class deviation and the CMMC route

findings.critique: For defence contracts the operative fact since May 2024 has been a class deviation directing contractors to Revision 2 instead of the edition in effect at solicitation, with assessment through the CMMC programme. The example mentions neither, so a contractor could conclude that Revision 3 applies to a new solicitation: the wrong-revision error the pattern exists to prevent. I could not confirm the deviation's status as of today.
findings.recommendation: Verify the current position on the DoD class-deviation page, then either add the deviation and the CMMC assessment route to this row or replace the DFARS illustration with a neutral one. Re-check the cited acquisition.gov link, which returned HTTP 404 when fetched on 2026-11-18.
